lessons.title: Feel the pulse as a cycle in your body before you count it
lessons.explanation: Counting is a description of a pulse, not the pulse itself. Open Music Theory's hypermeter chapter defines the tactus as the perceptual equivalent of a beat, the pulse a listener might tap a foot or nod along to, and it states plainly that a tactus is felt rather than notated. The same chapter demonstrates that when one passage is played at double speed or half speed, your tactus can settle on a different metrical level altogether, and it warns that at a very slow tempo the spans become too long to entrain to at all. That is the practical centre of this lesson. Meter is a hierarchy and not a row of equal clicks: beats group into bars, bars group into hypermeasures, and a listener entrains to one level as the tactus while the other levels remain subordinate. Subdivision is the act of cutting one beat into smaller equal parts, and it is not the act of adding extra events. A sixteenth note is a quarter note divided in four, so the division exists whether or not you play anything on it. When you feel the division as part of the same cycle as the beat, fast notes sound calm and even; when you count each division as a separate event, the pulse frays and the tempo drifts upward. The six lessons that follow all depend on this one distinction, so it is worth settling before anything is measured by a click.
lessons.example: Work in 4/4 at 72 beats per minute, where one beat lasts 0.833 seconds, one eighth note lasts 0.417 seconds, one sixteenth lasts 0.208 seconds, and one bar lasts 3.333 seconds. Four bars therefore occupy 13.333 seconds, which is your first hypermeasure. Step one, tap the beat with a foot at 72 and count one, two, three, four. Step two, keep the foot at exactly the same rate and say the sixteenths, one-e-and-a, without changing the foot. Step three, play four quarter notes in bar one and sixteen sixteenth notes on a single pitch in bar two, with the foot never moving. The sixteenths occupy the same 3.333 seconds as the quarters; nothing was added to the bar. Now change one variable and listen to what changes. At 60 beats per minute a beat is 1.000 seconds and a sixteenth is 0.250 seconds, so the same figure feels roomier, and at 90 beats per minute a beat is 0.667 seconds and a sixteenth is 0.167 seconds, so the same figure begins to sound busy. The notes did not change; the cycle did. A second diagnostic uses the hypermeasure. Play a four-chord loop, one chord per bar, at 72. At 3.333 seconds per bar, the whole loop is 13.333 seconds, and the fourth bar is hyperbeat four. If you place the loop's most conclusive chord anywhere except that fourth bar, the loop will sound as if it is being interrupted rather than finished, because you are contradicting a cycle that takes 13.333 seconds to complete.
lessons.question: A learner plays a bar of four quarter notes and then a bar of sixteen sixteenth notes at 72 beats per minute, and reports that the second bar is faster. Using the timing figures from this lesson, what is the accurate description?
lessons.answer: Both bars last 3.333 seconds; the sixteenths divide the same beat into four and the perceived speed belongs to the subdivision, not to the tempo
lessons.distractor: The second bar is genuinely faster because sixteen events per bar cannot fit into the same 3.333 seconds as four events
lessons.correction: One bar of 4/4 at 72 beats per minute is four beats at 0.833 seconds, which is 3.333 seconds, and that total does not depend on how many note values you place inside it. Sixteen sixteenths are sixteen divisions of the same 3.333 seconds, so each lasts 0.208 seconds. The tempo is unchanged and the density of events has changed, which is exactly the distinction between a felt cycle and a count of notes.

depth.definitions: The tactus is the felt pulse a listener taps or nods to; the source defines it as the perceptual equivalent of a beat, felt and not notated. A beat is the regular pulse counted inside a bar. A division or subdivision is a beat cut into two, three or four equal parts. Meter is the grouping of beats into bars with an implied accent hierarchy. A hypermeasure is a grouping of bars above the level of the bar; a hyperbeat is the corresponding pulse, where hyperbeat one coincides with the first bar of the group. Hypermeter is a perceived organisation rather than a notated one. Entrainment is the process by which a listener's or player's internal pulse locks to an external periodicity. Prerequisites are the counting of note values and rests from lesson 31, the meter work from lesson 21, and the quantisation and groove distinction from lesson 38.
depth.mechanism: A felt cycle works because perception tracks periodicity at several levels at once and promotes one of them to the tactus. That promotion depends on tempo: the source's own examples show the tactus moving between levels as a passage is played faster or slower, and it notes that at half speed the tactus and beat become so slow that the notated hypermeter is hard to perceive because the spans are too long to entrain to. Three consequences follow. First, accent in a metrical hierarchy is inferred from context, not from physical loudness, so a bar can be felt as accented even when nothing is played more loudly. Second, hypermeter is interpretational and can change with tempo, performance and the listener, so a disagreement about where a hypermeasure begins is not automatically an error by either party. Third, a screen shows equal spacing and therefore cannot show grouping at all: a piano roll at 72 beats per minute displays 0.417 seconds between eighths whether the passage feels like three groups of four or four groups of three. That is why the same loop can look identical at two tempos and feel entirely different.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting case is the same six eighth notes read in two different meters, because there the felt cycle changes while the note values do not. In 6/8 at 96 beats per minute the dotted-quarter beat is three eighths, so it lasts 0.938 seconds and the bar lasts 1.875 seconds; the count is one-and-a two-and-a, and the tactus normally falls on the two dotted-quarter beats. In 3/4 at 96, the quarter-note beat is 0.625 seconds, the bar lasts 1.875 seconds, and the count is one two three. The bar length and the pitches can be identical, and yet the first reading has two pulses per bar and the second has three. On guitar this is audible immediately: a strumming pattern built as down-down-up fits the 6/8 grouping, and the same pattern in 3/4 forces the hand to treat one of the three beats as a fresh beginning. The transferable lesson is that you cannot choose a grouping by counting louder somewhere; you choose it by deciding which cycle the body performs, and then the notation follows.
depth.mistake: Three misconceptions recur. The first uses counting aloud as a substitute for a felt pulse, so the internal tempo changes with the rate of speech; the diagnostic is to keep a foot or a nod at one fixed level while speaking the smaller divisions, and if the foot accelerates you have moved the tactus rather than subdivided it. The second treats each subdivision as a new event, which produces tension, uneven sixteenths and a tendency to arrive early at the next beat; the check is to play a bar of quarters and a bar of sixteenths and ask whether the foot moved at all. The third assumes the tactus must be the notated beat unit, so a slow movement at 50 beats per minute is counted in quarters and feels unresolvable; the source's own discussion of the tactus suggests moving the felt pulse to a faster level, which is what conducting in two or in four accomplishes. A learner who has decided in advance that 'slow music is harder' will reinforce the third error rather than test it.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, set a metronome to 60 beats per minute, where one beat is 1.000 second and one sixteenth is 0.250 seconds, and work in three one-minute blocks at that single tempo. In block one, tap the beat only and say nothing. In block two, keep tapping the beat and say the sixteenth syllables, one-e-and-a, for four bars. In block three, play one bar of quarters and one bar of sixteenths on a single pitch, foot unmoved, then repeat the pair with the count spoken silently. The rubric asks for the foot to remain constant across all three blocks, for the sixteenths to be even at 0.250 seconds without arriving early, for one written sentence that names the level you were entraining to, and for a clear statement of whether the sixteenth bar felt faster or merely denser. A model report reads: the foot stayed at 1.000-second intervals throughout; the sixteenths were even at 0.250 seconds; the sixteenth bar sounded busier but not faster; I was entraining to the beat, and when I stopped tapping the tendency was to push the sixteenths. If tapping a foot is uncomfortable, conduct with the hand or nod instead, and keep the same three-block structure.
depth.summary: A pulse is a cycle that your body performs and a count is a description of that cycle, and the two come apart whenever subdivision is confused with extra events. You now have a way to test which metrical level you are actually entraining to, and a set of timing figures at 60, 72 and 90 beats per minute with which to check your own playing without a machine. The next lesson takes the machine that everyone uses for exactly this job, the metronome, and asks what it is genuinely good for, what it cannot measure, and how to practise with a click without turning your playing into a grid.

visual.title: Feel the pulse as a cycle in your body before you count it — reasoning sequence
visual.description: One tempo, three metrical levels, and a four-bar cycle that decides where a loop can end.
steps: Fix the tempo: 4/4 at 72 BPM means one beat = 0.833 s, one eighth = 0.417 s, one sixteenth = 0.208 s.
Keep the tactus: tap the beat at 72 and speak the sixteenth syllables without letting the foot change rate.
Compare density, not tempo: bar 1 of quarters and bar 2 of sixteenths both occupy 3.333 s.
Extend the cycle: bar = 3.333 s, so a four-bar hypermeasure = 13.333 s and bar 4 is hyperbeat four.
Place the ending: a conclusive chord anywhere except hyperbeat four sounds like an interruption, not a close.

lessons.title: Practise with a metronome without turning your playing mechanical
lessons.explanation: A metronome is a reference periodicity, not a target you are aiming at. That distinction matters because the click is a tool you can configure, not a fixed truth. In FL Studio the metronome is a switch in the Options menu, Ctrl+M, and the manual describes its behaviour in one sentence: when enabled you hear a short metronome sound at the beginning of each beat and an accent at the beginning of each bar. The same manual note adds that the metronome options, including mixer track routing and changing the click sound, are on the Transport Panel. Two practical consequences follow. The click is a routed signal, so it can be balanced against your playing instead of shouting over it, and its sound can be changed to something you dislike enough to obey but not enough to follow blindly. Mechanical playing is not caused by the metronome. It is caused by treating the click as the goal, which flattens every event onto one level of emphasis and removes the small timing and dynamic variations that make a phrase speak. The way to keep the reference without becoming it is to change where the click falls and to spend part of each session without it. If you can only play the passage while the click is running, the click is carrying the pulse and your timing is being outsourced.
lessons.example: Take a four-bar loop at 72 beats per minute and design a twelve-minute session with computed figures. At 72, one beat is 0.833 seconds, one bar is 3.333 seconds, the loop is 13.333 seconds, and the loop repeats 4.5 times per minute. Block one, three minutes: click on every beat, play quarter notes on simple chords. That is 216 beats, and your attention should be on whether each attack lands with the click or slightly before it. Block two, three minutes: move the click so that it marks beats two and four rather than all four, which puts the reference 1.667 seconds apart and forces you to supply beats one and three yourself; this is the single most useful anti-mechanical setting, because half the time nothing is confirming you. Block three, three minutes: set a slow tempo of 60, where one beat is 1.000 second, and play eighths at 0.500 seconds against a click on the beat only. Block four, three minutes: click off, no count, play the loop four times and check at the end whether you are still aligned with the bar line you chose. A concrete result worth writing down is the difference between the first pass and the fourth: if the fourth pass has drifted, the pulse was being supplied by the machine. A second observation is diagnostic of the opposite problem. From the synchronization research cited below, people synchronizing with a metronome tend to anticipate the stimulus and tap slightly before it, and that tendency is less pronounced in trained musicians, so an experienced player who is a few tens of milliseconds early is not rushing; they are doing the normal thing.
lessons.question: A learner sets a click on every eighth note at 100 beats per minute to fix their timing on a swung shuffle, and reports that the groove has disappeared. What is the accurate account?
lessons.answer: Even eighths contradict a swung subdivision, so a click on every eighth forces the player toward evenness; the click belongs on the beat or on the backbeat instead
lessons.distractor: The click reveals that the groove was never accurate, so the player should keep the eighth-note setting until the pattern is even
lessons.correction: A swung eighth pair is notated as two equal eighths but performed unevenly, so a reference on every eighth asserts a subdivision the style does not use. At 100 beats per minute the beat is 0.600 seconds and the two eighths of a swung pair are performed unequally, for example 0.400 and 0.200 seconds, so a click at 0.300-second spacing lines up with neither note. Move the reference to the beat or to beats two and four and the feel returns while the tempo stays externally confirmed.

depth.definitions: A metronome is a device or a software function that produces a periodic click, usually with an accent marking the first beat of a bar. A count-in or precount is a bar or two of click before recording begins. Anticipation, described in the research literature as a tendency to tap slightly before the stimulus, means the player's attack precedes the click by a small margin rather than following it. Synchronization is the locking of a produced event to an external periodicity. Externalised timing means the pulse is supplied by a machine and fails when the machine stops; internalised timing means the player can sustain the periodicity alone. A grid is the equal spacing a sequencer displays, which is a representation rather than a feel. Prerequisites are the tactus and subdivision work from lesson 51, the honest-takes procedure from lesson 37, and the quantisation-versus-groove distinction from lesson 38.
depth.mechanism: Why does anticipation appear at all? The cited study models synchronization as a dynamical system in which an oscillator receives its own delayed activity as input, and reports that the anticipation tendency grows with longer stimulus periods up to 3500 milliseconds, that it is less pronounced in trained musicians than in non-musicians, and that it is influenced by external factors such as auditory feedback from one's own taps, the presence of a partner, and transmission latencies between coordinating partners. The practical implication is twofold. First, a very slow click is not automatically easier: a period of 3500 milliseconds corresponds to 17.14 beats per minute, and the source's own finding is that anticipation increases as the period lengthens, so a slow click can be harder to sit on than a moderate one; the usual fix is to click on a subdivision rather than on a much slower beat. Second, latency in a monitoring chain is part of the timing problem, not a moral failing, which is why the source discusses transmission latency between partners. The limits are equally important: a click measures onset timing only. It says nothing about tone, dynamics, the timing of releases, or whether the phrase breathes. A passage can be perfectly aligned to a click and still be unmusical, and a phrase with a deliberate push or pull can be musically strong and slightly off the click.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting application uses the same tool for a different job, and shows the metronome being used as a hypermetric marker rather than a beat marker. Take a sixteen-bar section at 84 beats per minute, where one bar is 2.857 seconds and sixteen bars are 45.714 seconds. If you set the click so that you hear only the bar accent and nothing on the other beats, you are not practising sub-beat accuracy at all; you are practising the hypermeasure and the section boundary, and the exercise is to know where you are in a 45.714-second span without being told four times per bar. A second version of the same idea is to start the click halfway through, so that your first task is to find the bar line from an arbitrary entry point, which is the skill needed to join a performance in progress. Compare this with the earlier example: a click on beats two and four trains the felt beat by removing confirmation, a click on the bar accent trains the hypermeasure, and a click on every eighth trains even subdivisions only. The same device supports three different competencies, and using one setting for all three is what makes practice feel monotonous and unproductive.
depth.mistake: Three errors are common. The first assumes the machine is always right and the player always wrong, so a passage that feels right is declared broken because it sits a few tens of milliseconds before the click; the cited study reports anticipation as a systematic property of synchronization that diminishes with training, so the diagnostic question is whether the offset is consistent and small rather than whether it exists. The second assumes that faster clicks are harder and slower clicks are easier, which the period finding contradicts at the slow extreme. The third practises only with the click and never without it, which externalises the pulse; the test is a click-free pass, and the remedy is the alternating block schedule in the example above. A quieter fourth error is forgetting that the click needs its own level in the mixer: at the default routing a loud click masks the quiet part of your own playing, and the manual specifically points to the Transport Panel for mixer track routing and click-sound settings.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, run three ninety-second segments at 60 beats per minute, where one beat is 1.000 second and one eighth is 0.500 seconds. Segment one uses a click on every beat; segment two uses a click on beats two and four only, so the reference arrives every 2.000 seconds; segment three has no click and no spoken count, and you mark where you believe the final bar line falls. The rubric asks for a stated outcome for each segment, a measured or honestly estimated drift at the end of the third segment, and one sentence distinguishing an offset you can hear in a recording from a fluctuation that changes within the passage. A model report reads: segments one and two held; in segment three the first two bars were steady and the third bar dragged, so the drift was in the second half of the loop, and I set the click on beats two and four for the next session. Label any figure you derive from a recording as measured, and label anything you estimate by ear as estimated; do not present an estimate as a measurement.
depth.summary: The metronome is a periodicity you can place anywhere, and its value comes from the placement you choose and from the passes you make without it. Anticipation is a normal feature of synchronization rather than an error, slow clicks are harder than they look, and a click that you cannot play without is a click you have outsourced to. With a felt pulse and a disciplined use of the click in place, the next lesson asks what happens when you deliberately play across the beat rather than on it, and why that displacement is the engine of groove rather than a mistake.

visual.title: Practise with a metronome without turning your playing mechanical — reasoning sequence
visual.description: The same click placed at four different points trains four different competencies.
steps: Configure the tool: metronome on (Ctrl+M), click sound and mixer-track routing set on the Transport Panel so the click is balanced, not loud.
Click on every beat: 72 BPM, 0.833 s apart, 216 beats in three minutes; this confirms but also confirms too much.
Click on beats 2 and 4: reference 1.667 s apart, so you supply beats 1 and 3 unaided; the strongest anti-mechanical setting.
Click on the bar accent only: 16 bars at 84 BPM = 45.714 s, which trains the hypermeasure and section boundaries.
Remove the click: play four passes unaccompanied and check whether the fourth still ends on your intended bar line.

lessons.title: Play across the beat on purpose: syncopation and groove
lessons.explanation: Syncopation is a controlled displacement of attacks relative to the meter, and it is the main reason a rhythm sounds like a style rather than a metronome. Open Music Theory describes the common pop form of it as straight syncopation: take a series of notes of equal duration, cut the first note's duration in half, and shift the remaining notes early by that half; a row of quarter notes all sounding on the beat becomes a note on the beat followed by notes on the offbeats. The chapter states that this process can happen at any metrical level and that the unit of syncopation is always half the duration of the straight notes, so beat-level syncopation shifts by a division and division-level syncopation shifts by a subdivision. A second family of patterns divides a unit into nearly even parts, and the chapter names the tresillo, the 3+3+2 grouping, as the common case. A third way to describe all of this is metrical dissonance, the terminology from Krebs that Open Music Theory adopts: displacement dissonance sets the same pattern against a different position in the meter, while grouping dissonance sets a grouping at a level where the meter does not group that way. Accent matters too, and the drum chapter defines the backbeat as the accent on beats two and four of a quadruple meter, which is a syncopation created by emphasis rather than by displacement.
lessons.example: Two computed cases fix the idea. Case one is the tresillo in sixteenths at 90 beats per minute. One beat is 0.667 seconds, so one sixteenth is 0.167 seconds, and a 3+3+2 group spans eight sixteenths: attacks at 0.000, 0.500 and 1.000 seconds, then the next cycle begins at 1.333 seconds. The third attack lands half a beat after beat two, an offbeat, and the group as a whole fills exactly two beats. Four bars of 4/4 at 90 hold sixteen beats, which is eight tresillo cycles, each 1.333 seconds, for a total of 10.667 seconds. Case two is grouping dissonance of three against four. Keep one attack every three sixteenths at the same tempo, so an attack every 0.500 seconds, inside a bar of sixteen sixteenths. Three and sixteen have no common factor smaller than the bar, so the pattern realigns with the bar line only after 48 sixteenths, which is three bars or 8.000 seconds, and that realignment contains sixteen attacks. Nothing about the pitches changed; the grouping simply refuses to agree with the bar for a full eight seconds, which is why the effect feels coiled rather than simply off. The backbeat is the quietest version of the same idea: at 90 beats per minute, an accent on beats two and four arrives every 1.333 seconds, exactly half the four-beat cycle of 2.667 seconds.
lessons.question: A learner plays a repeating pattern of attacks every three sixteenth notes at 90 beats per minute over 4/4 and wants to know when it will next coincide with a bar line. Using the figures from this lesson, what is the correct answer?
lessons.answer: After three bars, which is 8.000 seconds and sixteen attacks, because 48 sixteenths is the first point where the three-sixteenth grouping and the sixteen-sixteenth bar agree
lessons.distractor: After one bar, because any pattern played in 4/4 resolves at the end of the bar
lessons.correction: The bar contains sixteen sixteenths and the grouping advances in threes, so coincidence requires a multiple of both: the lowest common multiple of 3 and 16 is 48 sixteenths, which is exactly three bars at 2.667 seconds each, or 8.000 seconds. Calling it resolved after one bar treats the bar line as a reset that the pattern does not actually respect, which is precisely what grouping dissonance means.

depth.definitions: Syncopation is an accent or attack on a weak position of the meter, or the displacement of an expected attack. Straight syncopation is the specific transformation in which equal notes lose half the duration of the first note to a shift applied to the rest; its unit is half the straight duration. The tresillo is a 3+3+2 grouping of eight subdivisions. Metrical dissonance, following Krebs, is a conflict between sounding rhythm and metre; displacement dissonance sets a pattern at a different position within the metre, and grouping dissonance sets a grouping that the metre does not support. The backbeat is an accent on beats two and four of quadruple meter. Groove, in the research sense used here, is the property of music that induces movement, and the cited study operationalises it as ratings of wanting to move. Prerequisites are the subdivision and tactus work of lesson 51, the drum and backbeat material of lesson 36, and the quantisation-versus-groove lesson 38.
depth.mechanism: Syncopation works because the listener predicts the strong positions and the displaced attack arrives where the prediction expected nothing, so the ear tracks the metric hierarchy while the body follows the sounding rhythm. The research cited below supports a specific, bounded claim: in a web-based survey using funk drum-breaks with varying degrees of syncopation, medium degrees of syncopation produced the most wanting to move and the most pleasure, while entropy was a poor predictor of either, which the authors describe as an inverted U-shaped relationship that was stronger for participants who enjoy dancing. Three limits follow from that design. It is a rating study about drum-breaks rather than a claim about any particular piece, it measures self-reported desire and pleasure rather than movement itself, and the finding says nothing about whether a listener can play the pattern. A second limit comes from notation and production: because syncopation is a displacement, a quantiser set to a straight grid can move the displaced attacks back onto the grid and remove the very feature that carried the feel, so a groove that was played correctly can be destroyed afterwards by an edit that was intended to correct it.
depth.secondExample: Contrast displacement with grouping by taking one pattern and applying each in turn. Use a single chord played every eighth note at 90 beats per minute, so an attack every 0.333 seconds. Displacement keeps that spacing and moves the whole series so that its accents fall on the offbeats; the ear now hears the pattern late by half a beat while the bar stays where it was, which is the same relationship the metrical-dissonance chapter labels with a displacement sign. Grouping keeps the pattern's internal confidence but changes its length, for example accenting every third eighth, so that accents land one eighth later in each successive bar and the alignment drifts until it is restored after three bars, which at 0.333 seconds per eighth is 4.000 seconds for the full nine-eighth cycle. The two effects are audibly different: a displaced pattern feels like a deliberate push against a stable floor, whereas a grouped pattern feels like a wheel whose spokes do not match the axle. On guitar they are also practised differently, since displacement is a matter of where the strumming hand starts while grouping is a matter of how often the hand accents.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common. The first equates syncopation with being late or sloppy and practises it by dragging; the mechanism is a controlled shift relative to a maintained pulse, so the diagnostic is whether the underlying count is still steady and the displacement is measured in halves of a known unit. The second confuses displacement with a tempo change, so a bar of offbeat quarters is described as slower or faster rather than displaced. The third assumes accent always means volume, when the drum-chapter definition of the backbeat is about which beats carry the emphasis and accents in a groove are frequently produced by placement, duration and timbre. The fourth tidies the pattern on a grid and loses the point; check the quantiser setting before deciding that the performance was wrong, and remember the piano roll works at a fixed division, so a pattern that is deliberately ahead of or behind a grid line is being represented, not corrected. A useful diagnostic for all four is to count the pattern aloud against a click before editing anything.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task at 90 beats per minute, where one beat is 0.667 seconds, one eighth is 0.333 seconds and one sixteenth is 0.167 seconds, do three things in turn. First play one bar of straight quarter notes, twice, and confirm the attacks at 0.000, 0.667, 1.333 and 2.000 seconds. Second, play the straight-syncopated version of the same four events, where the first note is halved and the rest are shifted early by an eighth, so that you are deliberately on offbeats while the count continues. Third, play one tresillo cycle as sixteenths at 0.500, 0.500 and 0.333 seconds and tap the beat under it. The rubric asks for the count to remain audible or visibly steady, for correct durations in the tresillo, for one sentence naming which effect you produced, displacement or grouping, and for an explicit statement of whether a grid would have preserved or destroyed the pattern. A model report reads: the quarters were steady; the syncopated bar stayed inside the beat once I kept counting; my first tresillo was too even, so the 0.333-second note became a 0.250; I heard displacement rather than grouping. Finish by repeating the third item with the click on beats two and four, which is the setting from lesson 52 that removes most of the confirmation and exposes a real groove.
depth.summary: Syncopation is metre plus a stated amount of displacement, and groove is what that displacement does to a listener. You now have the vocabulary to separate displacement from grouping, computed figures for a tresillo and a three-against-four grouping at 90 beats per minute, and a clear reason to distrust a straight quantise on a part that was played with feel. The next lesson moves the same music to a different key, using the guitar's assumption that a chord is a movable shape, and the capo that turns that assumption into a transposition device.

readings.note: Re-read The Snare Drum and the Backbeat and the subsections Non-Snare Backbeats and Half- and Double-Time Feels. visual.title: Play across the beat on purpose: syncopation and groove — reasoning sequence
visual.description: Two families of syncopation, computed at 90 beats per minute, and a grid that can erase either one.
steps: Establish the units: at 90 BPM, beat 0.667 s, eighth 0.333 s, sixteenth 0.167 s, 4/4 bar 2.667 s.
Straight syncopation: halve the first of four equal notes and shift the rest early by that half, so attacks move to offbeats.
Tresillo: 3+3+2 sixteenths means attacks at 0.000, 0.500 and 1.000 s, cycling every 1.333 s; the third attack is half a beat late in metric terms.
Grouping dissonance: one attack every 0.500 s against a bar of sixteen sixteenths realigns only after 48 sixteenths = 3 bars = 8.000 s.
Backbeat: accents on beats 2 and 4 arrive every 1.333 s inside a 2.667-second bar, an emphasis syncopation with nothing displaced.

lessons.title: Play the same music in other keys: movable shapes and the capo
lessons.explanation: On a guitar, a chord is not a set of pitch names but a shape you place somewhere on the neck. That is why the same progression can be played in any key with the same fingerings, and why a song you learned in C can move to the key your voice prefers without learning anything new. This lesson makes the arithmetic explicit so that you are not guessing. Each fret is one semitone, so moving a shape up by n frets raises the sounding pitch by n semitones, which multiplies the frequency by 2 raised to the power n divided by twelve; one semitone is therefore a factor of about 1.0595. A capo is the same principle applied with a clamp. Fender's guide puts it as one of its six points about capos, describing the capo as a movable nut, and it notes that it can be removed without retuning the instrument, though it also advises tuning after taking the capo off. JustinGuitar makes the practical case even more directly: a capo lets you use the same chord shapes to play songs in different keys, singers use it to move a song into a key that suits the voice, and it is used to simplify songs that would otherwise demand barre chords, but it does not work for every song, and some songs still require barre chords. Two details determine whether the result sounds good. Place the capo just behind the fret, exactly as a finger should sit, or you get buzzing; and remember that clamping stretches the strings slightly, which is why tuning after removing the capo is not superstition.
lessons.example: Three computed cases on a 25.5-inch scale, which is 647.7 millimetres. Case one, the capo as arithmetic. With no capo, the open sixth string is E2 at 82.41 hertz. Move the same shape up one fret and the sounding key is F; up two frets, F sharp; up three frets, G. Check it: 82.41 multiplied by 2 to the power three twelfths gives 98.00 hertz, which is exactly G2. Move up five frets and 82.41 multiplied by 2 to the power five twelfths gives 110.00 hertz, which is A2. The shape never changed; only its position did. Case two, the physical distances involved, because they explain why a capo is not merely a convenience. On this scale the first fret sits 36.35 millimetres from the nut, the second at 70.66 millimetres, the third at 103.05 millimetres and the twelfth at 323.85 millimetres. A capo at the third fret therefore shortens every string's speaking length by about 103 millimetres and does the work that a barre at the same fret would do. Case three, choosing a key by range rather than by shape. If a melody tops out at A4, 440 hertz, in the key of C, and your comfortable ceiling is F4 at 349.23 hertz, then C is three whole steps too high for you and the natural fixes are to transpose the song down or to change the key while keeping the shapes that your hands already know; the two moves are equivalent in sound and different only in what your left hand has to do.
lessons.question: A learner wants to keep using the open E, A and D shapes they already know but needs the song to sound in G. Using the arithmetic in this lesson, what is the correct procedure?
lessons.answer: Place the capo at the third fret so the E shape sounds G, since three frets above E2 at 82.41 hertz is 98.00 hertz, which is G2
lessons.distractor: Place the capo at the fifth fret, because five frets above the open E shape is the G chord shape
lessons.correction: Each fret is one semitone, and three semitones above E2 is G2, confirmed by 82.41 multiplied by 2 to the power three twelfths, which equals 98.00 hertz. Five frets would put the E shape on A, at 110.00 hertz, because five semitones above E is A. The confusion in the distractor comes from counting chord names instead of semitones, and the fix is to count frets and check the resulting frequency.

depth.definitions: A transposition is a change of overall pitch level with the relationships between notes preserved. A movable shape is a fingering pattern that can be shifted along the neck, taking its sounding chords with it. A capo is a clamping device across the fretboard that shortens every string at once and works like a movable nut. A semitone is the smallest standard step on the neck, one fret, equivalent to 100 cents; a whole tone is two frets. Frequency rises with the twelfth root of two per semitone, and 2 raised to the power 1/12 is 1.05946. The scale length is the vibrating length from nut to bridge; on a 25.5-inch instrument it is 647.7 millimetres. Key is the tonal centre a passage is organised around. Prerequisites are the major key signatures and the order of sharps and flats from lesson 33, the chord-building of lesson 34, and the triad shapes from lesson 35.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is that pitch depends on vibrating length and tension, and shortening the string raises pitch in a fixed geometric progression. Because every string is shortened at the same fret, the intervals between the strings are preserved and any fingering pattern keeps its interval structure wherever it is placed, which is the whole reason guitar shapes are portable. Three limitations are worth stating. First, portability is not unlimited: a shape that uses open strings cannot move without changing its notes, which is exactly why a barre or a capo is needed to transport the sound of an open chord. Second, a capo changes which notes are available above it rather than the instrument's tuning, so melodies and open-string bass notes that used the nut stop existing in their original form. Third, the capo is a mechanical device with a physical cost: clamped too tightly, or seated too far from the fret, it raises the intonation slightly and produces buzzing, and the sources cited both advise attention to placement and to tuning after removal. A fourth, quieter limit is that a key chosen for its shapes is only the right key if the melody also fits; a key that suits your fingers can still be too high or too low for your voice.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the capo with the barre, which accomplishes the same pitch change by different means. Take the E shape at the third fret as before. A capo produces it by clamping at 103.05 millimetres from the nut and freeing all four fingers for other work; a barre produces it by pressing one finger across six strings, which requires that finger to span roughly 35 millimetres of string spread, about 7 millimetres between adjacent string centres on a 42-millimetre nut, and to hold all six down while the remaining fingers form the chord. The sounding result can be identical, and the physical demands are not: the capo requires no sustained pressure at all, which makes it the sensible choice for a song whose only obstacle is one barre chord, and the barre develops the finger strength and independence that a capo cannot. A second contrast is between transposing with a capo and transposing in a sequencer. In a piano roll, moving a part up three frets is the same as selecting it and transposing by three semitones, and the arithmetic is identical to the capo case: 82.41 hertz becomes 98.00 hertz. The difference is that the sequencer changes the sounding notes while the midi data can keep the original key, and a guitar part moved this way may become unplayable, because a shape that fits in one position may demand a stretch nobody has.
depth.mistake: Three misconceptions recur. The first treats the capo as a beginner's crutch; the guitar sources cited here both argue against that, and the practical reason is that the capo is the only way to keep open-string voicings in a different key. The second reports the wrong chord name because it confuses shape with sounding chord: with a capo at two frets, the shape the hand makes is a G shape and the chord a listener hears is A, and a bandmate told to play G will produce the wrong pitch. The diagnostic is to state both, shape and sounding chord, whenever a capo is in use. The third ignores setup: a capo placed far from the fret buzzes, an over-tightened capo pulls the strings sharp, and a capo left on while an instrument sits in a case. The fix is mechanical rather than musical, and the Fender guide's advice to tune after removing the capo is a reminder that clamping has a measurable effect on pitch. A fourth error is to assume that a lower or higher key is automatically easier to sing, when the only test is whether the melody's extreme notes sit inside your comfortable range.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, build a small capo chart before playing anything. Choose one progression you already own, for instance E, A, D and back to E, and write the sounding chords and the shape for three placements: no capo, capo three, and capo five. Use the arithmetic: three frets above E is G at 98.00 hertz, above A is C at 130.81 hertz, above D is F at 174.61 hertz; five frets above E is A at 110.00 hertz, above A is D at 146.83 hertz, above D is G at 196.00 hertz. Then play the progression in each placement at 80 beats per minute, where one bar is 3.000 seconds and the four-bar phrase is 12.000 seconds, and note which placement let you keep the strings ringing. The rubric asks for a correct chart in both shape and sounding names, correct frequencies for at least two entries, one sentence on fret-and-buzz behaviour, one sentence on which key suited your voice best, and an explicit note that you did not have to learn new fingerings. A model report reads: capo five turned E-A-D into A-D-G; the frequencies check out; I had to reseat the capo closer to the fret to stop a buzz on the third string; D was the comfortable key for singing. If a capo is not available, the identical exercise can be done by barring at the same frets, and the arithmetic does not change.
depth.summary: A guitar shape carries its intervals with it, so a key change is a position change, and the capo is the device that applies that shift without asking for sustained finger pressure. You can now compute the sounding key from the number of frets, name both the shape and the chord it sounds, and decide between a capo and a barre on physical rather than moral grounds. The next lesson takes the physical side seriously, because the barre is where beginners most often hurt themselves, and the question is not whether you can press hard but how to gain the ability without an injury.

lessons.title: Barre chords and the strength problem, approached safely
lessons.explanation: A barre is one finger pressed across several strings while the other fingers form the rest of the chord, and almost every learner who struggles with it concludes that they lack strength. That conclusion is usually wrong, and acting on it is how people injure themselves. What actually decides whether a barre sounds cleanly is leverage and placement rather than force: the index finger has to lie flatter than for a single note, rotated slightly so that the bony side of the finger contacts the strings, and its pressure is applied near the fret rather than in the middle of the fret space. The thumb sits behind the neck roughly opposite the index, providing a counter-force rather than squeezing, and the neck is often best angled slightly upward rather than held level. Classical guitar pedagogy has an exercise-based approach to this, and the barre materials cited here treat it as technique to be built in stages, not as a strength test. The safety side comes from clinical writing rather than from folklore. The University of Iowa's Music and Medicine material on guitar playing defines playing-related musculoskeletal disorders as weakness, numbness, pain, tingling or other symptoms that interfere with your ability to play at the level you are used to, reports that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk of injury in the study it cites, and states that symptoms require healthcare advice or treatment rather than a training plan. That sentence is the boundary for this lesson: the content here is practice design, not diagnosis.
lessons.example: Design a five-minute barre session with computed doses, because unbroken barre practice is the failure mode this lesson exists to prevent. Use a 4-second hold followed by an 8-second release, which is a 12-second cycle; five minutes is 300 seconds, so one set contains 25 cycles and 100 seconds of actual hold, a duty cycle of about 33 percent, with the remaining 200 seconds spent with the hand completely open. Three such sets in a day, six days a week, gives 18 sets and 1,800 seconds, which is 30 minutes of total barre contact time per week. Compare that with the plan most beginners attempt, which is twenty minutes of continuous barre chord practice: 1,200 seconds with essentially no release, and this is the version that produces soreness in the thumb, the wrist and the back of the hand. The Iowa material gives a rate for perspective that is worth reading carefully rather than quoting as destiny: it reports one injury per each 2,381 hours of practice, which at one hour a day is about 6.5 years, and at half an hour a day is about 13 years. The figure describes a population, not your hands, and the source's own practical finding is that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased injury risk, which is why the first two minutes of every session in this plan are spent on open chords and slow single notes rather than on barres. Geometry explains why the duty cycle matters. On a typical 42-millimetre nut the six strings are spread across roughly 35 millimetres, so the centres of adjacent strings are about 7 millimetres apart, and one straight finger has to cover five such gaps at once while its outer joints avoid muting strings it is not pressing. That is a placement problem, and placement improves with short accurate repetitions far faster than with long ones.
lessons.question: A learner practices six-string barre chords continuously for twenty minutes, feels numbness and tingling in the thumb, and decides to build strength by pressing harder. According to this lesson and the source it cites, what is the correct response?
lessons.answer: Stop and treat the numbness and tingling as a symptom requiring healthcare advice, then rebuild the barre with short holds, a release phase and a warm-up
lessons.distractor: Continue the twenty-minute sets but press harder, because numbness in the thumb is a normal stage of building barre strength
lessons.correction: The Iowa guitar-playing material defines playing-related musculoskeletal disorders as weakness, numbness, pain or tingling that interfere with playing at your accustomed level and states that such symptoms require healthcare advice or treatment, so numbness is not a training milestone. Pressing harder also attacks the wrong variable: a barre is decided by finger rotation toward the bony side, pressure close to the fret, and thumb counter-force behind the neck. A 4-second hold with an 8-second release is a 33 percent duty cycle and a far better dose than 1,200 seconds without release.

depth.definitions: A barre is a single finger stopping several strings simultaneously; a partial barre stops fewer strings than there are on the instrument. Placement means where along the fret space the finger presses. Leverage is the mechanical advantage produced by finger angle, thumb position and instrument angle rather than by muscular force alone. Warm-up is the low-demand playing at the start of a session before demanding material. A playing-related musculoskeletal disorder, abbreviated PRMD in the clinical literature cited, is defined by the source as weakness, numbness, pain, tingling or other symptoms that interfere with the ability to play an instrument at the level the musician is accustomed to. A duty cycle is the proportion of a period spent under load. Prerequisites are the chord change work of lesson 35, the capo and movable-shape arithmetic of lesson 54, and the setup awareness recorded in this course's earlier physical guidance.
depth.mechanism: The reason a barre fails is usually that pressure is distributed across too much finger surface at the wrong angle. A finger pressed flat with its soft pads facing the strings has a compliant contact that requires more force for the same result, while rotation toward the harder, flatter side of the finger creates a smaller, firmer contact patch and lets a straighter finger stay straight. Because adjacent string centres sit about 7 millimetres apart on a typical nut, a small change in angle moves the contact off a string entirely, which is why the symptom is usually a buzz on one string rather than a fully dead chord. Three limits belong with this. First, no practice design substitutes for setup: action, string gauge and neck relief all change how much force a barre needs, and a guitar that is hard to barre can be made easier without any change in technique. Second, the evidence cited is about injury rates in populations of players, so the specific figure of one injury per 2,381 practice hours should be read as context for caution rather than as a personal risk estimate. Third, this course does not diagnose; the source's own instruction is that symptoms need healthcare advice.
depth.secondExample: Contrast two routes to the same sounding chord and see how the safety arithmetic differs. A learner who needs G major in a song can barre at the third fret with the E shape, which in the schedule above means a 33 percent duty cycle with 100 seconds of contact in a five-minute set, or can place a capo at the third fret, which requires no sustained left-hand pressure at all and frees the fingers for the rest of the chord. The capo route removes the contact-time load entirely and is what the guitar-teaching sources cited in the previous lesson recommend for songs whose only obstacle is one barre. The barre route is the one that develops capability, and the sensible plan is to keep both: use the capo for repertoire so that pieces get finished, and use short dedicated barre sets so that the capability grows. A second contrast is between the barre and a three-string partial barre, which reduces the contact surface from five gaps to two, roughly 14 millimetres instead of 35, and is therefore the correct first exercise rather than a compromise. Progress from the partial to the full barre is measurable without a stopwatch: it is the point at which the full shape sounds clean for one 4-second hold without any change in finger angle.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common, and the first three interact. The first treats barre strength as the goal, so sessions get longer and harder instead of shorter and more accurate; the diagnostic is a duty cycle check, since anything much above a third of the time under load is a training plan built on a wrong theory. The second practices through numbness, tingling or a sharp pain that persists after stopping; the source is explicit that these are symptoms requiring healthcare advice, so the correct action is to stop and seek it. The third skips the warm-up, which is the one variable the cited study associates statistically with increased injury risk. The fourth reverses the physical setup: it raises the guitar neck too low and pulls the wrist into an angle that makes the barre impossible, then blames the hands. A quieter fifth error is treating the capo as a way to avoid ever learning a barre; both are useful, and the choice is a matter of which one the piece needs.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, warm up for two minutes on open chords and slow single notes, then run five minute-level sets inside the remaining three minutes: four seconds of hold followed by eight seconds of release, which is exactly 15 cycles, counting them out loud so that the release is as deliberate as the press. Use a partial three-string barre for the first three sets and the full six-string barre only for the last two. The rubric asks for the cycle count to be correct, for the release to be genuinely released rather than reduced in pressure, for the shape to sound clean at least once without changing finger angle, for one written sentence describing the contact point of the index finger, and for an honest note of any sensation that persisted after stopping rather than being treated as normal. A model report reads: warm-up on E, A and D for two minutes; 15 cycles with the press close to the fret and the thumb behind the neck; the fourth string buzzed until I rotated the index slightly; six-string barre clean on two of the last cycles; no numbness, mild thumb tiredness that passed within a minute. If any symptom in the source's list appears, stop the exercise and treat the next step as a healthcare question rather than a practice-planning question.
depth.summary: A barre is a placement and leverage problem that beginners misread as a strength problem, and the misreading produces the long unbroken sessions that hurt people. Short holds, real releases, a warm-up, partial barres first and a capo where the repertoire only needs one chord are a complete, physically sane route to the same capability. The next lesson moves the right hand to the centre of attention, where the thumb and the fingers have to run on different clocks at the same time, and where the same principle of small accurate repetitions applies to a very different problem.

questions.prompt: A learner plays a four-chord loop, one chord per bar at 72 beats per minute, and places the final chord at the end of bar three, arguing that the loop is complete because all four chords have sounded. Using the metrical hierarchy from lesson 51, what is the accurate account?
questions.answer: Four bars at 72 BPM form a 13.333-second hypermeasure, so ending in bar three interrupts hyperbeat four and the loop is heard as unfinished
questions.distractor: The loop is complete because every chord has sounded; the sense of incompleteness is a dynamic problem to be solved by playing the final chord more loudly
questions.correction: One bar at 72 beats per minute is 3.333 seconds, so four bars are 13.333 seconds and the fourth bar is hyperbeat four, the position where a group of four bars expects its close. Finishing in bar three leaves 3.333 seconds of an unfinished cycle, which is heard as interruption rather than as an ending. Loudness is a separate parameter and cannot supply the missing time.

questions.prompt: At 60 beats per minute a learner sets a click on every sixteenth note, so that the reference falls on every event they play. Which change best trains an internal pulse, and what is the resulting reference interval?
questions.answer: Move the click to beats two and four, which leaves an unattended reference every 2.000 seconds so the player must supply beats one and three
questions.distractor: Keep the sixteenth-note click and raise its level, because a denser and louder reference is always easier to follow
questions.correction: A click that coincides with every event confirms the player rather than testing them, so it cannot reveal an internalised pulse. At 60 beats per minute a beat is 1.000 second, so a click on beats two and four arrives every 2.000 seconds, exactly half of each four-beat bar, and the player has to produce the other two beats unaided. Raising the level of a dense click makes the dependency stronger, not weaker.

questions.prompt: A player records a tresillo on a keyboard at 90 beats per minute and then quantises the part to straight sixteenths to tidy the timing. What has happened to the pattern, described in the vocabulary from lesson 53?
questions.answer: The displacement has been removed: a profile of 0.500, 0.500 and 0.333 seconds becomes even sixteenths at 0.167 seconds, so the syncopation itself is gone
questions.distractor: The pattern has been converted from grouping dissonance into displacement dissonance, which preserves the feel at a finer metric level
questions.correction: At 90 beats per minute one sixteenth is 0.167 seconds, so a 3+3+2 grouping gives attacks at 0.500, 0.500 and 0.333 seconds; quantising to straight sixteenths replaces that asymmetry with equal spacing and removes the offbeat that carried the feel. The pattern was a nearly-even grouping rather than a displacement, and quantising cannot convert one category into the other; it can only flatten the timing.

questions.prompt: A learner puts a capo on the second fret and plays an A shape and then a D shape. Using the fret arithmetic from lesson 54, which chords sound, and at which frequencies for the bass notes?
questions.answer: The A shape sounds B with its bass at 123.47 hertz, and the D shape sounds E with its bass at 164.81 hertz, since two frets above A2 is B2 and two frets above D3 is E3
questions.distractor: The A shape sounds C at 130.81 hertz and the D shape sounds F at 174.61 hertz, because a capo on the second fret adds three semitones
questions.correction: Each fret is one semitone, so a capo at the second fret transposes by two semitones, a factor of 1.1225. A2 at 110.00 hertz becomes 123.47 hertz, which is B2, and D3 at 146.83 hertz becomes 164.81 hertz, which is E3. Both figures in the distractor correspond to three semitones rather than two, which is a capo at the third fret mis-counted as the second.

questions.prompt: A learner completes a five-minute session of continuous six-string barre chords and reports tingling in the thumb that persists after stopping, and asks whether to extend the session tomorrow. What does the material cited in lesson 55 support?

questions.distractor: The tingling is a normal stage of adaptation, so the session should be extended to ten minutes so the hand adjusts more quickly

The same source reports that failure to warm up was the one variable statistically associated with increased injury risk. A better dose is a 4-second hold with an 8-second release, which is about a third of the time under load, and a partial three-string barre before the full one.

units.title: Independence, lines and form: right-hand clocks, keyboard voicings, singing, a second section, and one finished performance

lessons.title: Fingerstyle basics: give the thumb and the fingers different clocks
lessons.explanation: In fingerstyle playing the right hand is doing two jobs at once, and the way to make them coexist is to give them different periodicities rather than to try to synchronise them. The thumb, called p in the classical abbreviations, usually takes the bass on the lower three strings; the index, middle and ring fingers, i, m and a, take the upper strings. Classical guitar pedagogy treats alternation between fingers as foundational rather than decorative: the alternation material cited here describes right-hand alternation as one of the most important concepts of right-hand fingering and notes that repeating the same finger by accident is a very common intermediate mistake, which is exactly the failure mode you get when the two clocks are not kept separate. A second technique question is which kind of stroke to use. In a rest stroke the finger comes to rest on the adjacent string; in a free stroke it moves clear of it. Playing a rest-stroke thumb with free-stroke fingers simultaneously is a genuine coordination problem, and the source's answer is essentially the plan for this lesson: the two techniques have to be learned separately, each has to be relaxed and predictable, and finger movement and planting, meaning preparing the finger on the string before releasing it, are what allow a simultaneous release. This connects directly to arrangement, because the texture chapter of Open Music Theory separates the functional bass layer from the melodic layer, and fingerstyle is the clearest physical demonstration of that separation on one instrument.
lessons.example: Build the pattern numerically so the two clocks are visible. Work at 72 beats per minute in 4/4, where one beat is 0.833 seconds, one eighth is 0.417 seconds and one bar is 3.333 seconds. Let the thumb play a steady quarter-note bass on the lower strings, so thumb attacks fall every 0.833 seconds on beats one, two, three and four. Let the fingers play eighth notes on the upper strings, alternating strictly, i then m then i then m, so finger attacks fall every 0.417 seconds; repeat the same finger only when the pattern demands it and never by accident. The two clocks therefore meet on every beat and diverge in between, and the meeting point recurs 72 times per minute. If you instead play four notes to the beat in the pattern p-i-m-a, each note lasts 0.250 seconds, which is 240 notes per minute at 60 beats per minute, and at that rate the alternation has to be automatic or the pattern will stutter. Now change one variable at a time. Halve the bass to one thumb note per bar, on beat one only, and the upper voice has twelve eighths of freedom to move in; keep the bass at quarters and move the upper part to sixteenths, and each 0.417-second alternation pair becomes a 0.208-second pair. Finally, test the simultaneous-stroke problem: play a rest-stroke thumb on the low E while the middle finger plays a free stroke on the top E. Both strokes must release on the same instant, yet one finger passes through the string and stops against its neighbour while the other lifts clear of it, and at 0.417-second spacing that decision recurs eight times in one 3.333-second bar, which is why the source cited below insists that each technique be relaxed and predictable on its own before the two are played together.
lessons.question: At 72 beats per minute a learner plays quarter-note thumb attacks and eighth-note finger patterns in 4/4, and reports that their fingers keep falling behind. Using the figures in this lesson, what is the correct diagnosis and remedy?
lessons.answer: The thumb runs at 0.833-second intervals and the fingers at 0.417-second intervals, so the fingers are twice as busy; slow the tempo or reduce the finger part to one note per beat until the alternation is automatic
lessons.distractor: The fingers are behind because the thumb is too loud, so the correct remedy is to play the bass more softly and the upper strings more firmly
lessons.correction: The two parts are not equally busy here: the thumb has four attacks per bar and the fingers have eight, at 0.833 and 0.417 seconds respectively, so the fingers have half the time per note. Balance does matter musically, but it does not fix a rate problem. The remedy is to reduce the finger part to the thumb's rate, or to lower the tempo, until the alternation happens without conscious decision, and then restore the eighth notes.

depth.definitions: Fingerstyle, or fingerpicking, means plucking with the fingers rather than a pick. The classical abbreviations for the right hand, from the Spanish names, are p for pulgar, the thumb, i for indice, m for medio and a for anillo. Alternation is the rule of using different fingers for successive notes on the same string rather than repeating one. A rest stroke, apoyando, finishes with the finger resting on the adjacent string; a free stroke, tirando, moves the finger clear of the strings. Planting, or preparation, is placing the finger on the string before it plays. The functional bass layer is the part that carries harmony and root motion; the melodic layer carries the foreground line, and the texture chapter of the source treats them as separate functions. Prerequisites are the alternation and picking work of earlier guitar lessons, the texture and layers material of lesson 35, and the metronome discipline of lesson 52.
depth.mechanism: Independence is easier to achieve when the two hands' parts have different periods, because the brain can chunk each stream separately and only has to reconcile them at their meeting points. That is why the thumb at 0.833 seconds and the fingers at 0.417 seconds are easier than two parts at the same rate with different accents: the first has one shared event per beat, while the second demands a decision on every attack. The mechanism also explains why planting helps. Preparing the finger on the string converts a timing task into a release task, so the moment of contact is no longer in question. The limits are worth stating. First, the same finger repeated on the same string is not always an error: some patterns deliberately repeat for tone or speed, and the alternation rule is a default rather than a law. Second, rest stroke and free stroke are not interchangeable on all strings, because a rest stroke physically ends against a neighbouring string, which cannot happen on the lowest or highest string in every pattern. Third, tension in the right hand is the usual cause of both uneven tone and speed ceilings, and the source's own answer to the hardest version of this problem is that each technique must first be relaxed and predictable before the two are combined.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the classical right hand with the keyboard, because the same musical problem appears there in a different physical form and shows which part of the difficulty is instrumental. On the piano, the left hand takes the bass and the right hand the upper part, and independence means each hand may move at its own rate without interference; there is no equivalent of a finger resting against a neighbouring string, and each finger is a small hammer rather than a plucking contact. A fingerstyle pattern such as p-i-m-a-i-m at 60 beats per minute, a six-note cycle of 0.250-second notes, has a direct keyboard analogue in a left-hand quarter-note bass under a right-hand six-note figure, and the two are learned by the same sequence of steps: the bass alone, the upper part alone, then both at a tempo slow enough that neither part degrades. The difference shows up in failure modes: on guitar, a wrong right-hand finger mutes or buzzes a string, whereas on the keyboard a wrong finger usually just plays the wrong note. That is why guitar alternation has to be practised for sound as well as for accuracy, and why this lesson has the thumb and the fingers on different clocks rather than the same one.
depth.mistake: Three errors recur. The first tries to make both hands run at the same rate from the beginning, which produces a part that stumbles whenever the upper line has more notes than the bass; the diagnostic is to say the pattern aloud at the same tempo, and if you cannot, the tempo is above the level at which the pattern is automatic. The second lets the same finger repeat by accident, which the alternation source names as a common intermediate mistake; the check is to watch the right hand for one bar and count the fingers used, then compare with the pattern's intention. The third practises everything with the right hand at maximum loudness, which masks muting and makes the two parts indistinguishable; the texture chapter's separation of a functional bass from a melodic layer is best demonstrated by making the thumb markedly quieter and slower than the fingers, which is a musical decision as well as a practice technique. A fourth, quieter error is holding the right hand pressed on the bridge, which produces unintentional palm muting and a thump instead of a note.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task at 60 beats per minute, where a beat is 1.000 second and an eighth is 0.500 seconds, work through four one-minute blocks on one chord pair. Block one, thumb only: quarter notes at 1.000-second intervals, listening for evenness. Block two, fingers only: eighth notes alternating i and m at 0.500-second intervals, listening for two distinct fingers. Block three, both together at the same rates, with the thumb deliberately quieter. Block four, the same combined pattern but with the finger part reduced to quarters so that the two parts run at the same rate, which should feel markedly easier and demonstrates the two-clock principle. The rubric asks for a correct statement of each part's period, for alternation with no accidental repeats in block two, for the two parts to remain distinguishable in block three, and for one sentence about whether your right hand tensed as rate increased. A model report reads: the thumb held 1.000-second quarters; the fingers alternated i-m at 0.500 seconds with one accidental repeat in the first bar; combining the two felt easier than expected; my wrist rose as I sped up, so I stopped and restarted slower. Note explicitly that no video or recording was made for this task, and that the check is your own listening.
depth.summary: Independence is easier when the parts have different periods, and the thumb and fingers can therefore be taught as two clocks that meet on the beat rather than as one stream that has to be split. You now have the alternation rule, the rest-stroke and free-stroke distinction, the planting habit that turns timing into release, and a numeric picture of how the two parts share a bar. The next lesson takes the same question of voicing into the keyboard, where changing which note is in the bass changes the feel of a chord without changing a single note of its content.

visual.title: Fingerstyle basics: give the thumb and the fingers different clocks — reasoning sequence
visual.description: Two periodicities in one bar at 72 beats per minute, and the meeting points that make the pattern learnable.
steps: Set the units: 72 BPM, so beat 0.833 s, eighth 0.417 s, bar of 4/4 3.333 s.
Thumb clock: quarter-note bass on beats 1 to 4, attacks every 0.833 s, four per bar.
Finger clock: eighth notes alternating i and m, attacks every 0.417 s, eight per bar.
Meeting points: the two clocks coincide on every beat, 72 times per minute, which is what keeps the pattern from drifting.
