lessons.title: Keyboard voicings: an inversion changes the feel, not the notes
lessons.explanation: An inversion puts a chord member other than the root in the bass. The notes are the same three, and yet the chord sounds different and behaves differently in a progression, because the interval from the bass to everything above it has changed. A C major triad is C, E and G; in root position the bass is C, in first inversion the bass is E, and in second inversion the bass is G, and the textbooks cited here label these with figures and, in lead-sheet notation, with slash chords such as C over E. Nothing about the chord's identity changes: the inversion chapter of Open Music Theory teaches spelling and identifying triads in inversion as the same triad with a different bass member, and it makes the point that the bass note is not the same thing as the chord's root. On a keyboard this is not a theoretical nicety but the main tool you have for making a progression flow, because you can usually move one or two notes instead of repositioning the whole hand. Two sources of guidance sit behind the practical part of this lesson. The orchestration chapter advises larger gaps in the bass register and smaller gaps higher up, with the densest packing in the middle, which is a warning against playing thick low chords. And the jazz voicings chapter, which treats spacing directly, notes that its examples keep the root in the left hand so that the harmony is always clear, while also observing that in performance the root is often omitted because the bassist supplies it.
lessons.example: Spell and measure the three positions of C major on a keyboard. Root position is C3, E3 and G3, at 130.81, 164.81 and 196.00 hertz. First inversion is E3, G3 and C4, at 164.81, 196.00 and 261.63 hertz. Second inversion is G3, C4 and E4, at 196.00, 261.63 and 329.63 hertz. The interval content above the bass is the thing that changed: in root position the bass carries a major third of 4 semitones and a perfect fifth of 7; in first inversion it carries a minor third of 3 and a minor sixth of 8; in second inversion it carries a perfect fourth of 5 and a major sixth of 9. Now measure the cost of moving between them instead of the distance between them. From root position to first inversion, if each voice moves to the nearest member of the next chord, the total motion is 4 plus 3 plus 5, which is 12 semitones spread across three voices; if instead you hold E and G and move only C up an octave to C4, the same change of inversion costs a single voice moving 12 semitones while the other two stay put. That second option is the one that keeps a progression smooth, and it is why inversions are a voice-leading device rather than a decoration. Register matters too: C4 at 261.63 hertz is exactly one octave above C3 at 130.81 hertz, and an octave is 1,200 cents, so a voicing moved up an octave keeps every interval inside it unchanged while transforming its weight. The range you are working inside is wider than most learners assume: an 88-key instrument runs from A0 at 27.5 hertz to C8 at 4,186.01 hertz, which is about 7.25 octaves, and the same triad can therefore be placed in registers that sound muddy, clear or thin.
lessons.question: A learner plays C, E, G and then moves the same three notes to E, G, C, and reports that they lost the chord because the root has gone. What is the accurate account?
lessons.answer: The chord is unchanged, C major in first inversion with E in the bass; the root is still C, since the bass note and the root are different things
lessons.distractor: The chord has become E minor because its lowest note is E, so the progression has changed key area
lessons.correction: E, G and C contain the same three pitch classes as C, E and G, so the triad is still C major; only its bass member has changed. The inversion chapter of the source states directly that the bass voice is not the same thing as the chord's root, and lead-sheet notation writes this chord as C over E to show both facts at once, the chord identity and the bass note. Calling it E minor would require a G sharp, which is not present.

depth.definitions: Inversion is the arrangement of a chord with a member other than the root in the bass. Root position, first inversion and second inversion place the root, third and fifth in the bass respectively. A slash chord, such as C over E, names the chord and the bass note separately. Figured bass is the older notation for the intervals above the bass. Voicing is the specific distribution of a chord's members across octaves and instruments, which is a different question from inversion. Doubling repeats a member, usually in another octave. Register is the octave area in which a part sounds. Prerequisites are the triads and Roman numerals of lesson 34, the inversion and bass-line material of lesson 44, and the arrangement and balance work of lesson 49.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism has two parts, one perceptual and one physical. Perceptually, the bass is the reference against which the listener measures the intervals above it, so a chord with E in the bass is heard as a stack of a minor third and a minor sixth rather than as a major third and a perfect fifth, even though the upper notes are identical; that is why the same three notes can sound stable, suspended or airy in different positions. Physically, on a keyboard, inversions allow a progression to be played with small hand movements, because adjacent chords can share members. The orchestration source adds a constraint that is easy to violate on a keyboard: large gaps belong in the bass and smaller gaps higher up, with the densest packing in the middle, so a low voicing with a widely spaced upper structure tends to sound muddy while the same spacing an octave higher sounds clear. Two limits should be kept in mind. First, this is a stylistic convention, not a law of acoustics: plenty of music deliberately places thick low chords for weight. Second, the jazz voicings chapter's observation that the root may be omitted in performance only holds when something else supplies that root, which is why the same chapter's written examples keep it in the left hand.
depth.secondExample: Contrast inversion with revoicing at the same bass note, because the two are often confused. Take a four-chord loop in C major, C, A minor, F, G. Using inversions, the bass can walk from C down to A and then to F and G without any bass note leaping an octave, which is the smooth version of the loop; each chord keeps its root among its notes and only the bass member changes. Revoicing instead keeps the same chord and the same bass and redistributes the upper members, for instance raising the fifth of F above the root or doubling the root an octave higher at 174.61 hertz instead of 349.23. The harmonic function is unchanged in both cases; what changes in the first case is the bass line and in the second case the spacing. A third, related contrast is between an inversion played by the left hand alone and the same inversion created by a collaboration: in a band, the keyboard can drop the root from its left hand because a bass instrument is already playing it, which is precisely the situation the jazz voicings chapter describes, while a solo keyboard arrangement usually needs the root sounding or the harmony becomes ambiguous to the listener.
depth.mistake: Three errors are common. The first hears a chord as its bass note and renames the chord accordingly, so C over E is called E minor or E something; the correction is to name both the chord and the bass, which slash notation does explicitly. The second assumes that inversion must be created by the bass instrument, so a chord whose lowest sounding note is the third but which is written as a root-position symbol is treated as an error; check what the score says rather than what the lowest note is, because the same chord can be notated either way. The third plays all inversions in the same register, usually low, and concludes that second inversion sounds worse than root position; the orchestration source's spacing guidance suggests moving the voicing up before judging it, and the frequencies show why, since a low cluster occupies the region where large gaps are wanted. A fourth, subtler error is to use inversions only as a way of avoiding hand movement, which produces a bass line that wanders; a bass line is a line, and it should be able to survive being played alone.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, take a four-chord loop you know, play it once in root position with the left hand as low as you normally place it, then play it three more times with a planned bass line built from inversions, writing the bass note under each chord. Keep a steady tempo such as 80 beats per minute, where one bar is 3.000 seconds and the four-bar loop is 12.000 seconds. Then sing or hum the bass line alone to hear whether it is a line rather than a series of jumps. The rubric asks for a written bass note under every chord, for correct interval counts above the bass in at least two chords, for one sentence on what changed in the feel when the bass moved, and for an honest note about whether any voicing sounded muddy and at which register. A model report reads: loop C, Am, F, G; bass line C, A, F, G on the low side of middle C; F in second inversion sounded hollow in that register, so I raised the whole voicing an octave and it cleared; the bass line worked as a line and I could sing it. Do not describe this as having produced a recording; the deliverable is a written analysis plus a pass you listened to.
depth.summary: An inversion keeps every pitch and changes the reference point, which alters the intervals a listener measures, the smoothness of a progression and the register the chord occupies. You now have the three positions of a triad spelled with frequencies, the interval content above each bass note, the voice-leading cost of moving between them, and the spacing rule that separates a clear voicing from a muddy one. The next lesson adds the voice itself to the two hands you have already coordinated, which is a heavier demand on attention than either hand alone, and it comes with its own physical cautions.

visual.title: Keyboard voicings: an inversion changes the feel, not the notes — reasoning sequence
visual.description: One triad, three bass notes, and the intervals above the bass that a listener actually measures.
steps: Root position: C3 E3 G3 at 130.81, 164.81 and 196.00 Hz; intervals above the bass are 4 and 7 semitones.
First inversion: E3 G3 C4 at 164.81, 196.00 and 261.63 Hz; intervals above the bass become 3 and 8 semitones.
Second inversion: G3 C4 E4 at 196.00, 261.63 and 329.63 Hz; intervals above the bass become 5 and 9 semitones.
Count the movement, not the positions: root position to first inversion totals 12 semitones if every voice moves, or 12 in one voice if the other two are held.
Place, then judge: larger gaps low and smaller gaps high, and an octave anywhere is 1,200 cents, so register changes weight without changing intervals.

lessons.title: Sing while you play: solving the coordination problem
lessons.explanation: Playing an instrument and singing at the same time asks one body to run two performances that both compete for attention, and the way through is to make one of them cheap. That is not a motivational slogan; it follows from how the tasks overlap in the brain. A study of singing and cello playing, cited below, reports that the two activities recruit partially overlapping brain networks, which is a precise way of saying that they share resources rather than living in separate compartments. Anything that reduces the cost of the accompaniment, by making it automatic, frees capacity for the voice, and anything that keeps the accompaniment effortful will keep the singing unstable. The practical consequences are mostly about sequencing. Learn the accompaniment until it runs while you are talking to someone; sing the melody by itself until the pitches are reliable and the words are no longer a reading exercise; mark the breath points at phrase ends before you combine the two; then put them together one phrase at a time, at a tempo slow enough that neither part degrades, adding a phrase per session. Two physical cautions belong at the front rather than at the end. Singing is a physical activity with its own failure signals, and the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders lists hoarseness or raspiness, losing the ability to hit high notes you could previously sing, a throat that feels raw, achy or strained, and finding talking an effort, and it advises that a voice problem should be assessed by a doctor, often an ear, nose and throat specialist. It also lists ordinary care: stay hydrated, take vocal naps, and use a humidifier when the air is dry. Pushing your voice to compete with an instrument is the commonest avoidable mistake in this lesson.
lessons.example: Work with a 32-bar piece at 84 beats per minute, where one beat is 0.714 seconds, one bar is 2.857 seconds and the whole piece is 91.429 seconds, about one minute and thirty-one seconds. Take a four-bar phrase, which is 11.429 seconds. If the melody moves at roughly two syllables per beat, that is 32 syllables in 11.429 seconds, about 2.8 syllables per second, while a strumming right hand playing one attack per beat produces 16 attacks in the same span, about 1.4 per second. The voice is therefore doing twice as many events as the hand, and if you try to consciously supervise both streams the slower one will stutter. This is the argument for automating the hands rather than the voice, which is the opposite of what most beginners attempt. Now budget the breath. A phrase lasting 11.429 seconds needs at least one breath at its end, and the cheapest place sits on a beat you are not singing, where a beat is 0.714 seconds; place that gap at the phrase boundary rather than mid-phrase and the melody keeps both its shape and its air. Finally, set a realistic dose: twenty minutes on six days a week is 120 minutes of practice per week, and inside it, combining one four-bar phrase for three minutes costs 12 minutes for the whole piece, leaving time for the accompaniment alone and for the singing alone, which are the two blocks that determine whether the combination works at all. If the voice tires rather than the hands, the source's advice is hydration, rest for the voice, and an assessment by a clinician rather than more repetitions.
lessons.question: A learner can play the accompaniment and can sing the melody, but the two fall apart together, and resolves to fix it by practising the combination harder and louder until it locks. What is the better plan, and why?
lessons.answer: Automate the accompaniment first, then combine one phrase at a time at a slow tempo, because singing and playing recruit partially overlapping networks and the combination only works when one part costs little attention
lessons.distractor: Sing more loudly so the voice becomes the dominant task, because the two parts simply need equal energy to lock together
lessons.correction: The research cited here reports partially overlapping brain networks for singing and playing an instrument, so the two tasks compete for shared resources; the reliable fix is to reduce the cost of one of them, not to raise the energy of both. Singing louder adds force to an activity with its own strain signals, which the NIDCD lists, including a throat that feels raw or achy. Meanwhile the arithmetic favours automating the hands: in a four-bar phrase at 84 beats per minute the voice may produce about 2.8 events per second against the hand's 1.4.

depth.definitions: Coordination here means performing two streams whose events do not coincide. Automatisation is the stage at which a motor sequence runs with little conscious supervision. A breath point is a planned gap in the vocal line. Vocal strain is the sensation of effort associated with phonation, and the NIDCD's warning signs include hoarseness or raspiness, loss of previously available high notes, a throat that feels raw, achy or strained, an effort to talk and repeated throat clearing. A phrase is a unit of melodic thought, whose shape and breathing are treated in the melody and phrasing chapter of the source. Prerequisites are the phrase-shaping and release work of lessons 22 and 46, the fingerstyle independence of lesson 56, and the rehearsal analysis from lesson 37.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms are in play. The first is resource competition: if singing and playing overlap in the networks that plan and execute the two actions, then improving one part by attention alone leaves less of that attention for the other, which is why the failure is usually in the part that is least automatic at that moment. The second is that motor sequences become cheap with repetition and stay expensive when they are still being constructed, so the ordering of practice matters more than the total time. The cited study is a neuroimaging comparison of singing and cello playing and describes partial overlap, which is a claim about shared recruitment rather than a claim that one task blocks the other; it does not measure practice outcomes and should not be read as predicting how quickly anyone will learn. The NIDCD material has different limits again: it is public health information on voice care and warning signs, not a treatment plan, and it directs voice problems to a clinician. Between them, these two sources support the sequencing advice in this lesson and the instruction to stop and seek assessment when warning signs appear, and neither supports a promise that a particular practice routine will produce a particular result.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a hand pattern that is easy to sing over with one that is not, using the same melody and tempo. A steady one-chord-per-bar accompaniment at 84 beats per minute gives the voice 2.857 seconds between harmonic events, so no coordination decision is required at the moment of a chord change beyond keeping the hand on schedule. Shift the same harmony to two chords per bar, so a change every 1.429 seconds, and every syllable that lands at a change point now requires the voice and the hand to agree on timing, which doubles the number of coordination events per phrase from 4 to 8 without changing a single note of the melody. Apply the same reasoning to the keyboard: a left hand playing block chords once per bar interferes far less with singing than an arpeggio pattern at 0.4-second spacing, because the arpeggio has more internal decisions. The transferable rule is to reduce the number of simultaneous decisions first and the tempo second, and only then to add the ornamentation that makes the part musically interesting. When the combined version runs, restore the busier pattern at the same tempo and the phrase usually holds.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common. The first learns both parts simultaneously from day one, so neither ever becomes automatic and every session re-solves the same coordination problem; the diagnostic is whether the accompaniment can run while you talk, and if it cannot, the combination is premature. The second sings louder to overcome the instrument, which adds effort to the one stream that has documented strain signals; the fix is to play more quietly, which is a musical choice you can make freely. The third ignores breath placement and then blames the voice for running out, when a phrase of 11.429 seconds at 84 beats per minute simply needs a planned gap at its end. The fourth practises always in the same seated position, hunched over the instrument, and never tests standing or a straighter posture; the singing apparatus needs the ribcage and neck to be free, which is a posture question rather than a talent question. A quieter fifth error is to assume that a good performance must be checked by recording every attempt, which turns practice into auditioning and, at high monitoring levels, adds an unnecessary hearing risk.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task, choose a two-bar vocal phrase from a song you can already play. Minute one: the accompaniment alone at 84 beats per minute, with a bar of 2.857 seconds, until it feels automatic. Minute two: the melody alone, unaccompanied, with the breath point marked at the phrase end. Minute three: combine at 60 beats per minute, where a bar is 4.000 seconds, one phrase at a time. Minute four: return to 84 and repeat the phrase three times. Minute five: write the breath point and one sentence about where coordination broke down, naming the moment rather than the part. The rubric asks for a stated breath point, for the phrase to survive three consecutive passes at tempo, for a specific description of the difficult moment, and for a note on whether the voice felt relaxed or effortful; if the voice felt strained rather than merely tired, the next step is the care advice in the source, not another repetition. A model report reads: the accompaniment ran while I counted in my head; the breath sat after the fourth bar; the hard moment was the chord change under the third syllable; three passes held, so I added the fourth bar of the phrase. Do not describe any part of this as recorded or as played back; it is a practice plan you can run yourself.
depth.summary: Singing while playing is a resource problem before it is a talent problem, and the reliable route is to make one stream automatic, plan the breathing, and add the combination one phrase at a time at a tempo that survives it. Voice care is part of the lesson rather than an appendix: hydration, rest and a clinical assessment if the warning signs appear. The next lesson turns from performing a section to writing one, and asks how a second section can belong to the first while changing enough to be worth hearing.

Combine at reduced tempo: 60 BPM gives a 4.000-second bar, then restore 84 once the phrase survives three consecutive passes.

lessons.title: Write a second section that belongs, and change the arrangement without adding a track
lessons.explanation: A second section has to be recognisable as part of the same piece while being worth hearing as a change. The method is to hold several parameters constant and move two or three decisively. Hold the tempo, the phrase length, the tonic and at least one melodic or rhythmic idea; move the harmonic schema, the register, the density, the rhythmic surface, or the loudness. The form chapter cited below gives the vocabulary and the scale: sections in popular music are typically eight to twenty-four bars, a core section carries the main material while an auxiliary section such as a bridge exists to create contrast, and the text warns that the relationships between sections are frequently not clear cut, which is permission to work by ear rather than by rule. Changing the schema is one of the strongest levers available, and the four-chord schemas chapter shows that the same four chords read in a different rotation produce a recognisably different loop with a shared vocabulary. Arrangement contrast without adding tracks is mostly a matter of voicing rather than instrumentation, and the orchestration chapter splits the problem usefully: simultaneous or vertical decisions cover how chords are voiced, how lines are doubled and what texture results, while successive or horizontal decisions cover effects such as a crescendo. Register, doubling, density and a level change are all available to one part. The last of these has a number attached: plus or minus 6 decibels doubles or halves amplitude, and a 6-decibel lift spread across eight bars at 90 beats per minute, which is 21.333 seconds, is about 0.281 decibels per second.
lessons.example: Build a piece from an eight-bar A section at 90 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.667 seconds and eight bars are 21.333 seconds. A is one chord per bar, four notes in the voicing, melody in the middle register, no dynamic change: duration 21.333 seconds. Now write B as a variation rather than a new song. Keep the tempo at 90, keep the phrase length at eight bars, keep the tonic, and keep the melody's opening three-note shape. Change exactly three things. First the schema: if A rotates a four-chord loop in the order one, five, six, four, then B rotates the same four chords as six, four, one, five, which the four-chord schemas chapter describes as a rotation of a schema, so the vocabulary is shared and the emphasis is not. Second the register: lift the upper part by one octave, which is 1,200 cents, so the intervals inside the voicing are identical and only their weight changes. Third the texture and density: A has one chord per bar with four notes, B moves to two chords per bar with three notes each, so the harmonic rhythm doubles from an attack every 2.667 seconds to one every 1.333 seconds while the total number of sounding notes falls, which is contrast in rhythm and density rather than in quantity. Then handle the dynamic yourself rather than with an extra part: lift the level by 6 decibels across the whole of B, which at 21.333 seconds is about 0.281 decibels per second, and the piece has a section change that a listener can hear without a single new instrument. The form A B A then runs 21.333, 21.333 and 21.333 seconds, or 64.000 seconds in total, and the return of A is audible because the register, harmonic rhythm and level all fall back together.
lessons.question: A learner writes a B section that keeps the tempo and phrase length, doubles the number of notes, raises the level and adds a new layer, and complains that the piece now sounds like one long section. What is the diagnosis?
lessons.answer: Nothing in B changed in kind, only in amount, so the section adds weight rather than contrast; change a schema, a register or a rhythmic surface while holding the rest constant
lessons.distractor: The B section is too short, so it should be extended to twice the length of A before the contrast can register
lessons.correction: Doubling the notes, raising the level and adding a layer all increase intensity while leaving the musical parameters that define a section unchanged, so the listener hears A performed louder rather than a different place in the form. Contrast comes from changing something categorical: the schema's rotation, the register by an octave, or the rate at which harmony moves from one chord every 2.667 seconds to one every 1.333 seconds. Length is a separate question, and the form chapter's typical range of eight to twenty-four bars suggests the eight-bar length was already defensible.

depth.definitions: Form is the large-scale organisation of a piece into sections. A core section carries the primary material and an auxiliary section, such as a bridge or an intro, supports or contrasts with it. A schema is a stock progression with its own rotation; rotating a schema means reordering the same chords so that a different chord begins the loop. Harmonic rhythm is the rate at which chords change. Register is the octave area of a part, and an octave is 1,200 cents. Density is the number of sounding events or notes per unit of time. Voicing is how a chord's members are distributed. Vertical or simultaneous orchestration concerns chords, doubling and texture; horizontal or successive orchestration concerns change over time, such as a crescendo. Six decibels corresponds to a doubling of amplitude and minus six to a halving. Prerequisites are the function and schema work of lessons 41 and 14, the form and boundary material of lesson 47, and the automation work of lesson 48.
depth.mechanism: Contrast works when the listener can hold the unchanged parameters as a frame and hear one parameter move against it; if everything moves, the frame is lost. That is why the form literature describes auxiliary sections functionally rather than by content, and why the same chapter warns that the relationships are often not clear cut: the analysis is an interpretation of a perception, not a property stored in the notes. Loudness-based contrast has a specific mechanism worth separating from the others. A 6-decibel rise is an amplitude ratio of about 1.995, so the ears register it as a clear increase in level, but loudness is also affected by register and density, which means a section lifted an octave may need no level change at all and a section that keeps its register may need several decibels before it reads as louder. Two limits follow. First, level changes push a mix toward clipping as everything approaches the ceiling, which is why the subtractive approach of lesson 49 exists. Second, if the contrast is produced only by level, a listener who hears the piece quietly will lose the form entirely, so register, schema and rhythmic surface are the more durable levers.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the arranged version with the performed version, because the same contrast can be created without touching a level control. On guitar, the same four-chord progression can be played as open-position strums with the strings ringing, and then as muted, single-note arpeggios in a higher position; the change in attack and register arrives from the hands rather than from automation, and it costs no extra track. On the keyboard, the first section can be played with both hands thickly in the middle register while the second drops the left hand out and moves the right hand up an octave, which reduces density and raises register at once, again from performance alone. Compare that with the automated version: a 6-decibel rise over 21.333 seconds, about 0.281 decibels per second, is drawn once and then repeats identically, which is precisely the difference between the automation and event-data material of lesson 48. Neither route is superior; the performed version can vary between takes and therefore sounds more like a player, while the automated version is reproducible. What matters is that you choose a categorical parameter to move rather than adding another layer, because a layer changes quantity and a parameter change changes place.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common. The first writes a second section with no shared material, so it sounds like an excerpt from a different piece; the diagnostic is to list what is held constant, and if the list is empty the section is not yet part of this piece. The second writes a section that only adds: more instruments, more notes, higher level, which is a dynamic climax rather than a formal contrast. The third assumes automation is the only way to create dynamics, when a player's own control of touch and velocity does the job and comes with the performance; note the distinction between MIDI velocity, which is a note-on parameter that changes how an instrument responds, and a level change in decibels, which changes the audio itself. The fourth changes the harmonic rhythm and the register and the schema and the tempo all at once, which is a different song rather than a new section. A quieter fifth error is to place the new section at a length that unbalances the form; with sections between eight and twenty-four bars, a B of thirty-two bars will dominate a twenty-four-bar A, and the form chapter's own proportions suggest checking the balance deliberately rather than by feel.
depth.application: For a five-minute nonblocking task at 90 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.667 seconds, write two four-bar sections on paper and then play them. Four bars is 10.667 seconds each, and the pair is 21.333 seconds. In section one, fix the schema, the register and the density. In section two, hold the schema's chords, the tempo and the phrase length, and change exactly two parameters from this list: schema rotation, register by an octave, harmonic rhythm from one chord per bar to two, density from four notes to three, or a level change of 6 decibels, which across 10.667 seconds is about 0.563 decibels per second. The rubric asks for a written list of what was held and what moved, at least one computed figure with its unit, the total duration of the pair in seconds, and one sentence describing what a listener would notice first. A model report reads: held tempo, phrase length and chord vocabulary; moved the rotation to start on the sixth degree and raised the upper part an octave, which is 1,200 cents; the pair runs 21.333 seconds; a listener would notice the register change first. Label any level change you write as a target in decibels rather than as a measurement, because nothing here was rendered or metered.
depth.summary: A second section belongs when most parameters hold still and two or three move category rather than quantity, and arrangement contrast is available through register, doubling, density and level without any new track. You now have the tools to write B rather than to add to A, and to state which parameter you changed and why. The final lesson in this level takes one piece all the way through rehearsal and capture, with an honest account of what a recording can and cannot tell you.

lessons.title: Rehearse and record one piece from start to finish
lessons.explanation: This lesson is the level's capstone: take one piece, rehearse it in a stated order, capture it, and write down what you actually have. The rehearsal order matters more than the total time, and the practical advice from the recording literature is straightforward: be prepared before you press record, and treat your monitoring level as something to keep comfortable because you are acting as your own engineer. That second point is a hearing question rather than a mixing preference; the World Health Organization's campaign material on safe listening exists because unsafe listening practices put over one billion young adults at risk of permanent, avoidable hearing loss, as its hearing-loss fact sheet states. Two technical distinctions carry through the whole process. The first is MIDI against audio: MIDI.org's introduction to the protocol describes MIDI as instructions rather than sound, so a MIDI file is a set of instructions for a sound source, while an audio render is the sound itself. The second is that rendering is not the same act as saving, and the export documentation notes that the master mixer track is rendered by default and that MIDI is not an audio format. Everything in this lesson is described as a procedure you run and then check by listening; no project was opened, no file was rendered and no sound was heard while the lesson was written, and every number below was computed rather than measured.
lessons.example: Plan a 45-minute session for a 32-bar piece at 84 beats per minute, where one beat is 0.714 seconds, one bar is 2.857 seconds and the piece is 91.429 seconds long. The numbers first. A two-bar count-in is eight beats, which is 5.714 seconds. Six takes of 91.429 seconds total 548.6 seconds, which is 9.14 minutes of recorded material. Three listening passes over one take are 274.3 seconds, or 4.57 minutes. Storage, if you keep the takes as uncompressed audio, is determinate: 44,100 samples per second in two channels at two bytes per sample is 176,400 bytes per second, so 91.429 seconds occupies about 16.13 megabytes, and at 48 kilohertz and 24 bits, which is 288,000 bytes per second, the same take is about 26.33 megabytes. The session then divides as follows. Twenty-eight minutes of preparation before the first take: ten minutes of warm-up and chunk work on the two hardest passages, because failure to warm up is the one variable the clinical guitar source in lesson 55 associates with increased injury risk, then eight minutes on the boundaries between chunks, played slowly enough that the joins are indistinguishable, and ten minutes of work on the entry, which is the bar most likely to be rushed. Ten minutes of full takes with the count-in, which is six takes at 91.429 seconds plus six count-ins of 5.714 seconds, about 9.71 minutes of playing. Nine minutes of listening back, which is three passes. The remaining minutes go to the take log, which is the deliverable that makes the session useful: for each take, write the tempo, the take number, the two most audible problems, whether the problem is technical or musical, and whether the take is usable. Select by listening rather than by memory of playing, because a take that felt excellent often has a wrong note at the first chord change and a take that felt anxious often sounds settled.
lessons.question: A learner finishes a session with six recorded takes, remembers that the fourth felt best, deletes the rest and sends the fourth. What is wrong with this procedure?
lessons.answer: Selection by memory of the performance is unreliable, so the takes should be listened to before deciding, with a written log naming each take's audible problems
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong; the take that felt best is the best take, and deleting the others saves storage
lessons.correction: The recording is the evidence and your memory of a performance is a separate, less reliable trace of it; nervous and confident feelings do not track audible accuracy closely, which is why the procedure is to listen back and write down what you hear. The six takes total 9.14 minutes of material at 91.429 seconds each, and three listening passes cost 4.57 minutes, which is a small price against the risk of discarding the take that actually worked. Storage is not a reason either: one take is about 16.13 megabytes at 44.1 kHz and 16-bit stereo.

depth.definitions: A take is one complete recorded pass. A count-in or precount is a bar or two of click before recording begins. A render is the production of an audio file from a project, which the export documentation distinguishes from saving the project itself. Audio is a representation of sound over time; MIDI is a set of instructions, as the protocol's own overview states, so a MIDI file does not contain sound. A take log is a written record of each pass with the problems it contains. Monitoring is the act of listening to what you are recording. Safe listening, in the WHO's usage, concerns both the level and the duration of exposure. Prerequisites are the count-in and honest-take discipline of lesson 37, the automation work of lesson 48, the balance procedure of lesson 49, and the rendering and delivery-note material of lesson 50.
depth.mechanism: Why rehearse in chunks with overlapping boundaries? Because a piece fails at its joins, and a join is only rehearsed when the two chunks are played together; a run-through that starts at the top every time spends most of its repetitions on material that is already secure. Why is a take log more useful than a feeling? Because listening is a different task from playing, and the two produce different information: playing engages motor memory and expectation, while listening engages perception of the recorded result. Why does the file-size arithmetic matter? Because it makes the cost of keeping several takes concrete rather than a vague worry, so that the decision to keep or discard is made on evidence. Two limits belong here. First, a recording exposes errors and does not improve the performance; if the piece is not rehearsed, more takes produce more evidence of the same problem. Second, the monitoring level affects both your hearing and your judgment of balance, which is why the guidance is to keep it comfortable and to give the ears breaks rather than to use volume as a substitute for a good performance.
depth.secondExample: Contrast a deliberately layered capture with a single live pass, because the choice changes what you can honestly claim. In a single live pass, one recorded take contains the guitar, the keyboard and the voice together, and every balance decision is performed by the player: the file is a document of a moment, and its imperfections are part of the result. In a layered capture, each part is recorded separately, which allows parts to be checked individually and mistakes to be replaced, at the cost of needing a click, headphones and a monitoring plan, and at the further cost that a performance assembled from parts may have less coherent timing than a single pass. Both are legitimate; the mistake is to describe the layered version as one performance. A related contrast is between keeping the takes as audio and exporting a MIDI file instead of an audio file: the MIDI export is instructions for a sound source and contains no sound, so it cannot be handed to someone as a recording, which is the distinction the protocol overview and the export documentation both support. Whichever route you choose, the delivery note should say which one it was.
depth.mistake: Four errors are common. The first never records because the piece is not yet perfect, which delays the one activity that reveals what needs work; the corrective is a low-stakes session whose purpose is a log, not a release. The second chases one perfect take and stops after twenty minutes of retries, when the documented behaviour of a take log is that the best take is usually not the one that felt worst or best. The third monitors loudly, which flattens perception, tires the ears and, on the WHO's evidence about unsafe listening practices, carries a real hearing risk. The fourth confuses a MIDI export with an audio render and sends a file that produces no sound on the recipient's machine; the distinction is the one the protocol overview is written to make, and it is worth stating explicitly in the delivery note which kind of file you produced. A quieter fifth error is not writing down the tempo, key and take numbers, so that a good pass cannot be found again.
depth.application: For a time-boxed session, reproduce the 45-minute plan above on one piece: ten minutes of warm-up and chunk work, eight minutes on joins at a slow tempo, six minutes of full takes with the count-in, nine minutes of listening, and the remainder for a written log. When you write the log, state for each take the tempo in beats per minute, the two audible problems, and whether each problem is technical, meaning execution, or musical, meaning intention. The rubric asks for a correct count-in duration for your tempo, a computed storage figure for one take at a stated sample rate and bit depth, a logged evaluation of at least three takes, one sentence separating what you expected to hear from what you heard, one sentence on monitoring level and ear breaks, and an explicit statement of whether the deliverable is a single pass or a layered assembly. A model report reads: 84 BPM, so a two-bar count-in is 5.714 seconds; one take is 91.429 seconds and about 16.13 megabytes at 44.1 kHz 16-bit stereo; takes two and five were usable, three had a rushed third phrase; I expected take four to sound best and it did not; monitoring stayed comfortable with a break every fifteen minutes; the deliverable is a single live pass. Every figure in that report is either computed or heard by you, and none of it was produced by this lesson.
depth.summary: Rehearsing in chunks with overlapping joins, capturing several takes, listening before deciding and logging what you heard is a complete finishing procedure that needs no new equipment and no new theory. The distinctions that keep the process honest are MIDI against audio, rendering against saving, and what a recording can and cannot tell you about your playing. Together with the level's earlier work on felt time, syncopation, transposition, physical safety, right-hand independence, voicings and singing, this closes a sequence that began with a pulse you can feel and ends with a piece you can hand to someone with a truthful note attached.

questions.prompt: At 96 beats per minute a fingerstyle player's thumb sounds one bass note per bar while the fingers play eighth notes above it. What are the two intervals, and what does the ratio imply for practice?
questions.answer: The thumb fires every 2.500 seconds and the fingers every 0.313 seconds, so the finger part carries eight times as many events and must become automatic on its own before the parts are combined
questions.distractor: Both parts run at the same interval of 0.625 seconds, because at any tempo the thumb and the fingers should share the beat
questions.correction: One bar of 4/4 at 96 beats per minute lasts 2.500 seconds, so a single thumb note per bar recurs every 2.500 seconds, while an eighth note lasts 0.313 seconds. That is a ratio of eight to one, which is exactly the situation in which the busier stream must be practised alone until it needs no supervision. Making both parts share the beat would remove the contrast the texture chapter treats as the point of separate bass and melodic layers.

questions.prompt: A keyboardist plays F, A and C, and then plays F, A and C again an octave higher, describing the second voicing as an inversion that has changed the bass. Which description is correct under the inversion material of lesson 57?
questions.answer: Both chords are F major in root position; the second is the same voicing raised by 1,200 cents, and an inversion would need A or C in the bass
questions.distractor: The second chord is F in second inversion, because raising a voicing by an octave changes which chord member is heard as the bass
questions.correction: An inversion is defined by which member is in the bass, so F major in root position has F in the bass, first inversion has A, and second inversion has C. Moving the same three notes up an octave leaves all three pitch classes in place and keeps F in the bass, so the chord is still root position; the change is one of register, where an octave is 1,200 cents. The distractor treats height as if it altered function, which would make every octave doubling a chord change.

questions.prompt: A learner can sing the melody reliably alone and can play the accompaniment reliably alone, but the combination fails at every chord change. Which plan follows the evidence cited in lesson 58?
questions.answer: Automate the accompaniment, plan the breath points, and combine one phrase at a time at a reduced tempo, because the two tasks recruit partially overlapping networks and one of them has to become cheap
questions.distractor: Sing more loudly and play more firmly so that each part is strong enough to survive on its own, since overlapping tasks simply need more energy from both
questions.correction: The singing-and-cello study describes only partial overlap between the networks involved, which means the two tasks share some planning and execution resources; if the accompaniment is still under construction it consumes those shared resources, and the failure appears exactly where coordination decisions cluster, at chord changes. Raising the energy of both parts adds strain to the voice, whose warning signs the NIDCD lists, and does not reduce the number of simultaneous decisions; halving the harmonic rhythm, one chord per bar instead of two, is the cheaper first step.

questions.prompt: A songwriter's second section matches the first in tempo, phrase length and chord vocabulary, but listeners report no sense of arriving somewhere new. Which single change best creates the missing contrast while keeping the section related?
questions.answer: Move a categorical parameter: rotate the schema so a different chord begins the loop, or lift the upper part by an octave, which is 1,200 cents
questions.distractor: Add a further layer and a doubled octave at a higher level, because contrast is produced by more content than the first section had
questions.correction: Rotating a four-chord schema is documented as a rotation rather than a new progression, so the vocabulary stays shared while the emphasis moves, and a register change of 1,200 cents alters weight without touching intervals. Adding layers and raising the level increase intensity, which a listener hears as the same section performed more heavily; the form chapter's core-and-auxiliary distinction is about a section doing a different job, not about doing more of the same job.

questions.prompt: A learner exports a MIDI file of the finished piece and sends it as the recording, telling the recipient to listen to the performance. What is the problem, and what does the file contain?
questions.answer: A MIDI file holds performance instructions rather than sound, so the recipient needs a sound source; only an audio render is a recording
questions.distractor: The MIDI file holds audio at a lower resolution, so the recipient will hear the piece but with reduced quality
questions.correction: The protocol overview describes MIDI as instructions for a sound source, and the export documentation adds that a MIDI file is not an audio format, so there is no sound inside the file to hear at any quality. The distinction matters because it is invisible in a file listing: both files may be a few hundred kilobytes and both open in the same application, and only one of them plays without an instrument or a software synthesizer behind it.

questions.prompt: A player practises a slow ballad with a click at 40 beats per minute and finds they are consistently ahead of the click, by a wider margin than when they practise at 100 beats per minute. Using the synchronization evidence in lesson 52 and the timing arithmetic of lesson 51, which explanation is defensible, and what is the practical fix?
questions.answer: Anticipation grows as the stimulus period lengthens, and 40 BPM gives a 1.500-second period against 0.600 seconds at 100 BPM, so the slow click is the harder one and the fix is to click on a subdivision
questions.distractor: The slow click is not trackable, so the player is guessing; the fix is to raise the metronome level until the click is unmistakable
questions.correction: The cited study reports that the anticipation tendency increases with longer stimulus periods up to 3500 milliseconds and is less pronounced in trained musicians, so a slower click is expected to produce a larger anticipation, not a smaller one. At 40 beats per minute a beat is 1.500 seconds and at 100 it is 0.600 seconds, which is the same finding expressed in this lesson's units. Raising the level does not change the period; clicking on eighths gives a 0.750-second reference at 40 and a 0.300-second reference at 100, which restores the difficulty relationship the player was testing.

questions.prompt: A recorded keyboard tresillo is played back for two assistants at 90 beats per minute. One wants to quantise the part to straight sixteenths to correct 'untidy' timing, the other wants to leave it. Which arithmetic settles the dispute, and what would the correction actually change?
questions.answer: The tresillo attacks fall at 0.500, 0.500 and 0.333 seconds inside a 1.333-second cycle, so quantising to sixteenths at 0.167 seconds replaces a deliberate asymmetry with even spacing and destroys the syncopation
questions.distractor: Quantisation is harmless because sixteenths are finer than the pattern's grid, so the part can only become more accurate
questions.correction: Finer is not the same as more accurate: a 3+3+2 sixteenth grouping contains durations of 0.500, 0.500 and 0.333 seconds, and straight sixteenths fix each event at a multiple of 0.167 seconds, which removes the 0.333-second note and with it the offbeat that gave the pattern its feel. The research cited in lesson 53 found that medium degrees of syncopation produced the most wanting to move among listeners, which is evidence that this asymmetry is the feature rather than the defect, though it is survey evidence about listeners' ratings rather than a claim about this particular take.

questions.prompt: A guitarist with a capo at the third fret plays an E shape, and a keyboardist plays G major as G3, B3 and D4. Comparing the guitar's lowest sounding note with the keyboard's, which part sounds higher, by what interval, and what are the frequency figures?
questions.answer: The keyboard part is higher: G3 at 196.00 hertz against the guitar's G2 at 98.00 hertz, which is an octave or 1,200 cents above
questions.distractor: The guitar part is higher, because the capo shortens the strings and pushes the guitar to 196.00 hertz against the keyboard's 98.00 hertz
questions.correction: Three frets above E2 at 82.41 hertz is 98.00 hertz, which is G2, so the capo'd E shape sounds in the octave below the keyboard's G3 at 196.00 hertz; an octave is a frequency ratio of two, which is 1,200 cents. The distractor reverses the direction and ignores the octave numbering, and the check is arithmetic rather than impression: 82.41 multiplied by 2 to the power three twelfths is 98.00, and doubling 98.00 gives 196.00.

questions.prompt: A learner plans a 45-minute session on barre-heavy repertoire with headphones at a loud monitoring level, no warm-up, and continuous barre passages. Identify the two risks that the sources cited in this level actually name, and state the fix for each.
questions.answer: Failure to warm up, which the clinical source associates with increased injury risk, and loud listening, which the WHO material treats as an unsafe practice carrying hearing risk; the fixes are a warm-up with short loaded holds and comfortable monitoring with breaks
questions.distractor: The only risk is running out of time before the session ends, so the fix is to lower the repertoire's tempo and skip the listening pass
questions.correction: The Iowa guitar-playing protocol reports that failure to warm up was the only variable statistically associated with increased risk of injury in the study it cites, and it directs symptoms to healthcare advice rather than to more practice. The WHO's safe-listening campaign addresses level and duration together, and its hearing-loss fact sheet states that over one billion young adults are at risk of permanent, avoidable hearing loss from unsafe listening practices. Session length is a scheduling matter and neither source names it as an injury factor; the duty cycle of short holds with genuine releases is what manages the physical load.

questions.prompt: A learner sings a melody in eighth notes while strumming quarter notes at 84 beats per minute and finds the singing is the part that collapses. Using the coordination reasoning of lesson 58 and the independence reasoning of lesson 56, what is the correct account of the load, and the first change to make?
questions.answer: The voice is running at 0.357 seconds per event against the hand's 0.714 seconds, so it is doing twice the work; simplify the accompaniment to one attack per bar, then rebuild the rate once the phrase holds
questions.distractor: Both streams should be speeded up to the same 0.357-second rate, because matching the two rates is what removes interference between them
questions.correction: At 84 beats per minute a beat is 0.714 seconds, so an eighth-note vocal line has an event every 0.357 seconds while quarter-note strums arrive every 0.714 seconds: the voice carries twice the density. Forcing both streams to the faster rate multiplies the coordination decisions instead of reducing them, which is the opposite of what the shared-resource finding in lesson 58 implies. Simplifying the accompaniment to one attack per bar, which is 2.857 seconds, leaves the voice to be the only fast stream, and the bar can be restored once the phrase survives repeated passes.

questions.prompt: A swing tune is played at 100 beats per minute, where one beat is 0.600 seconds. One practitioner sets a click on every eighth note and another sets a click on beats two and four. Which setting supports the feel, and what is the timing reason?
questions.answer: Beats two and four, because a swung pair is performed unevenly and an even 0.300-second reference asserts a subdivision the style does not use
questions.distractor: Every eighth note, because more frequent references always improve timing accuracy, and skilled players perform a swung pair evenly
questions.correction: A swung eighth pair is notated as two equal eighths and performed unequally, so a click at 0.300-second spacing falls between the two performed notes and pulls the player toward an even subdivision; the swing chapter of Open Music Theory describes swing eighths as a groove in which even notation is realised unevenly, and the backbeat is an accent on beats two and four. A reference on beats two and four arrives every 1.200 seconds, which is sparse enough to leave the pairing to the player while still fixing the tempo.

questions.prompt: A piece has an eight-bar A section followed by a sixteen-bar B section at 90 beats per minute, with the B section built by doubling the harmonic rhythm and lifting the register an octave. State the two section durations and identify which of the changes is a hypermetric contrast of length rather than a change of surface.
questions.answer: A is 21.333 seconds and B is 42.667 seconds; the doubling of length is the hypermetric contrast, while the faster harmonic rhythm and the octave lift change surface and register without altering the hypermetric spans
questions.distractor: A is 21.333 seconds and B is also 21.333 seconds, because a section's length is set by its phrase count rather than by its bar count
questions.correction: One bar at 90 beats per minute is 2.667 seconds, so eight bars are 21.333 seconds and sixteen bars are 42.667 seconds. Hypermetre concerns spans at the level above the bar, so doubling the number of bars doubles the span the listener is entraining to, which is the contrast of length. Raising the register by 1,200 cents and moving from one chord every 2.667 seconds to one every 1.333 seconds both act inside those spans, which is why they can be heard as a change of surface while the section boundary remains where the bar count put it.

questions.prompt: A song in G demands one barre chord, and the learner can place a capo at the third fret and use the open E, A and D shapes instead. Using the physical arithmetic of lesson 55 and the transposition arithmetic of lesson 54, what does each route cost and what does each develop?
questions.answer: The capo removes sustained left-hand pressure by clamping 103.05 millimetres from the nut, so it suits unfinished repertoire, while the barre builds capability through short loaded holds at roughly a third of the time under load
questions.distractor: The capo is a shortcut that prevents the barre from ever developing, so it should be avoided until the full barre can be held continuously for a minute
questions.correction: A capo at the third fret shortens each string's speaking length by about 103.05 millimetres on a 25.5-inch scale and requires no sustained finger pressure at all, which is why both cited guitar-teaching sources treat it as a legitimate device for repertoire that would otherwise need a barre. The barre is not something a capo prevents; it is a separate skill trained by a 4-second hold with an 8-second release, about 33 percent of the time under load, up to the point where a full-shape barre sounds clean without a change in finger angle. Holding a barre continuously for a minute is precisely the long unbroken dose the clinical source's findings argue against.

questions.prompt: To make a second section sound different without adding an instrument, a player moves the same three-note voicing up an octave and doubles the root an octave below. Which parameters have changed, which have not, and what figure states the register change exactly?
questions.answer: Register and density change while every interval inside the chord stays identical, because the octave shift is 1,200 cents and the pitch classes are unchanged; the doubling adds weight, not new harmony
questions.distractor: The chord's inversion has changed because the lowest sounding note moved, so the second section performs a different harmonic function
questions.correction: An octave is a doubling of frequency, which is 1,200 cents, and it preserves the ratio between every pair of notes, so the chord's intervals and its identity are untouched; what changes is the register the chord occupies and how many strings or keys are sounding. Adding a root an octave below increases density and weight, which the orchestration chapter treats under doubling rather than under harmony. The distractor confuses a register change with an inversion, but an inversion requires a different chord member in the bass, and moving everything up together keeps the same member lowest.

questions.prompt: A 32-bar piece at 84 beats per minute is exported, and the resulting audio file is 94.929 seconds long rather than 91.429 seconds. Which explanation is most likely, and what should be checked before treating the difference as a performance problem?
questions.answer: The render length follows a hierarchy that includes a tail setting, so the file is longer than the musical material by about 3.5 seconds; check the render-length and tail settings first
questions.distractor: The extra 3.5 seconds mean the performance ran at about 80.9 beats per minute, so the tempo must have been set incorrectly before recording
questions.correction: Thirty-two bars at 84 beats per minute is 128 beats at 0.714 seconds each, which is 91.429 seconds, and the export documentation describes a render-length hierarchy in which a tail is included, so a file that runs past the material is expected behaviour rather than evidence of a wrong tempo. The tempo implied by the distractor is computed as 7,680 divided by 94.929, which is about 80.9 beats per minute, and a genuine tempo error of that size would be audible as a slower performance throughout rather than as silence added at the end. Check the settings and the head and tail of the file before changing anything about the performance.

questions.prompt: At 60 beats per minute a fingerstyle pattern has the thumb on the beat and the fingers on eighths, while the sung melody moves at two syllables per beat. Which stream should be simplified first, and what are the three intervals involved?
questions.answer: The finger part, because it runs at 0.500 seconds, exactly the same rate as the voice at 0.500 seconds, while the thumb is at 1.000 seconds; reduce the fingers to the thumb's rate first
questions.distractor: The voice, because the voice is always the stream to simplify, and it should be reduced to one syllable per beat regardless of what the hands are doing
questions.correction: At 60 beats per minute the beat is 1.000 seconds, so the fingers on eighths produce an event every 0.500 seconds and a two-syllable-per-beat melody also produces one every 0.500 seconds. Two streams at an identical rate conflict at every event, which is the configuration lesson 56 warns against, whereas the thumb at 1.000 seconds is already the sparse stream that anchors the bar. Reducing the fingers to the thumb's rate leaves the voice as the only fast stream and the pattern still keeps its two-layer structure; simplifying the voice would remove the melodic detail without reducing the coordination load, since the fingers would still be at 0.500 seconds.

questions.prompt: A learner scores twelve out of twelve on this level's test questions and concludes that they can now perform, sing and record the piece to a usable standard. Which judgement is accurate, and what would count as evidence?
questions.answer: The score is not evidence of playing, singing or recording competence; the evidence is a recorded pass judged by listening, with a written log of what was heard and what remained unresolved
questions.distractor: Twelve correct answers establish the competence, because the questions required application rather than recall and covered every lesson in the level
questions.correction: These questions are binary-choice checks of reasoning, and even a perfect score says only that the reasoning was available at that moment; they cannot test finger independence, vocal coordination or whether a take is usable. The evidence this level asks for is concrete: a pass of the piece at a stated tempo, a count-in that matches the arithmetic for that tempo, a take log naming each pass's audible problems and whether the problem was technical or musical, and an explicit statement of what was expected compared with what was heard. Label any figure derived from a recording as measured and anything estimated by ear as estimated.
